Commentary on Matthew

For they broaden their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes; they love also the first places at table at dinners and the first chairs in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace and to be called rabbi by men. Woe to us wretches, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have passed! The Lord, when he had given the commandments of the law through Moses, added at the end: You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be unmoved before your eyes; and the sense is: Let my precepts be in your hand, that they may be fulfilled in deed; let them be before your eyes, that you may meditate on them day and night. The Pharisees, interpreting this badly, used to write the decalogue of Moses, that is, the ten words of the law, on little strips of parchment, folding them up and binding them on the forehead and making as it were a crown for the head, so that they might always move before their eyes, as the Indians and Babylonians do to this day; and whoever has this is judged among the peoples to be, as it were, religious. Moses had also commanded another thing: that they should make violet-blue fringes on the four corners of their cloaks to distinguish the people of Israel, so that, as circumcision in their bodies gave a sign of the Jewish nation, so their clothing might have some distinction. The superstitious teachers, courting popular favor and pursuing gain from silly women, used to make large fringes and bind very sharp thorns in them, so that, namely, as they walked and sat they might now and then be pricked and, as by this reminder, be drawn back to the duties of God and the ministries of his service. Since, therefore, the Lord had said: They do all their works in order to be seen by men, what he had charged in general he now divides into parts. Those little slips of the decalogue they called phylacteries, because whoever had them would have them as it were for his own guarding and protection, the Pharisees not understanding that these things are to be carried in the heart, not on the body; otherwise bookcases and chests too have books, and do not have the knowledge of God. This, among us, superstitious little women do to this day with little Gospels and with the wood of the cross and things of this kind, women who have indeed a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, straining out the gnat and swallowing the camel. Of this kind was the fringe, small and short, prescribed by the law, which that woman also who suffered a flow of blood touched on the Lord's cloak; but she was not pricked by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees, but rather was healed at its touch.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 12

But what should be said of those who love the first couches at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues and the first greetings in the marketplace and to be called Rabbi by men? Clearly offenses of this kind were found, and are found, not only among the scribes and Pharisees of that time alone, but even in the Church of Christ there are found not only banquets, and those who, undertaking the tables of those who provide them, but also those who love the first seats at them and do many things — first, indeed, that they may become deacons (not such as Scripture describes, but such as are "those who devour the houses of widows, praying at length for a pretext," and who for this reason "shall receive the greater judgment"). And those who wish to become deacons of this sort consequently strive to seize beforehand the visible first seats of those who are called presbyters. Some, however, not content even with these, contrive very many things, so that they may be called bishops by men (which is Rabbi), when they ought to understand that a bishop must become "beyond reproach" and the rest of the things that follow, so that even if he is not said to be a bishop by men, he may nevertheless be one before God. For he who has in himself the things which Paul enumerates concerning a bishop, even if he is not a bishop before men, is a bishop before God — even if he has not come to that rank through the ordination of men. For in this way a man is a physician who has learned the medical discipline and is able to heal as a physician: even if the sick do not entrust their bodies to him, he is a physician. But also a man is a pilot who has learned the pilot's art and is able to use it as is fitting: even if no one has entrusted to him the helm of a ship, he is nevertheless a pilot.

But you will find lovers of new glory who are zealous for glory from men and do not desire it from God; and, as it were, some men are brought before them as before judges and governors; and, if it must be said, through this very thing they make Christ's lightest burden an intolerable burden. But the disciple of Christ bears with it and still intercedes and does all things that he may be seen by God, despising human glory. He, seeing the suppers of the Gospel parables and the heavenly churches and assemblies and fairs of the firstborn, in which was (according to the Song of Songs) the bride, loves indeed at the spiritual suppers the first couches, that he may eat the better portions of the spiritual foods and the first-fruits of the spiritual banquet, and not the leftovers of the rest. He loves also, with the apostles sitting "upon twelve thrones", the first seats, hastening to render himself worthy by good deeds of seats of this kind; and so too the greetings which take place in the fairs, which we explained above. But the just man loves to be called Rabbi neither by men nor by any other, certain that there is one master of all. And all who are under him are, one toward another, brothers. But also he who by a heavenly birth has been born not only "of water" but also "of the Spirit", and has received "the spirit of adoption", so that it may be said of him that he was born not "of flesh" "nor of the will of man but of God", still being the son of none of those who are reckoned on earth and below, does not call anyone father on earth, as one who through every deed accomplished according to God says "our Father, who art in heaven". And if anyone ministers the divine words, he by no means offers himself to be called master, as one knowing that Christ is in him when he has made good progress, whom it behooves to be called master by all who have been benefited, but he professes himself a minister according to the commandment of Christ, who says: he who is greater among you, let him be the minister of all. Since Christ himself also, though he was truly master, professed himself to be a minister, saying: "but I am in the midst of you, not as one who reclines at table, but as one who ministers."

But well, after all the things by which he forbade the desires of vainglory, did he add, saying: he who exalts himself shall be humbled. Would that all indeed heard this, but most of all deacons and presbyters and bishops — most of all those who suppose that these things are not written for them: he who exalts himself shall be humbled. For which reason, as though not knowing that other saying either, he who humbles himself shall be exalted, they do not hear him who said: "learn of me, for I am gentle and humble of heart". But they are puffed up, and through their inflation they fall "into the judgment of the devil", and they do not seek through humility to ascend from the judgment of inflation, when they ought to remember the word of wisdom which says: "the greater you are, the more humble yourself, and before God you will find grace". And this the Lord first fulfilled; for as much as he had been great, so much did he humble himself. For "though" he "was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of man; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself even unto death, and death of the cross. For which reason God also exalted him above all, and gave him a name which is above every name" and the rest.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

But they not in these only, but in other little things, suffered from this disease.

For, "they love," He saith, "the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi." For these things, although one may think them small, yet are they a cause of great evils. These things have overthrown both cities and churches.

And it comes upon me now even to weep, when I hear of the first seats, and the greetings, and consider how many ills were hence engendered to the churches of God, which it is not necessary to publish to you now; nay rather as many as are aged men do not even need to learn these things from us.

But mark thou, I pray thee, how vainglory prevailed; when they were commanded not to be vainglorious, even in the synagogues, where they had entered to discipline others.

For to have this feeling at feasts, to howsoever great a degree, doth not seem to be so dreadful a thing; although even there the teachers ought to be held in reverence, and not in the church only, but everywhere. And like as a man, wherever he may appear, is manifestly distinguished from the brutes; so also ought the teacher, both speaking and holding his peace, and dining, and doing whatever it may be, to be distinguished as well by his gait, as by his look, and by his garb, and by all things generally. But they were on every account objects of ridicule, and in every respect disgraced themselves, making it their study to follow what they ought to flee. For they love them, it is said; but if the loving them be a matter of blame, what a thing must the doing them be; and to hunt and strive after them, how great an evil.
Commentary on Matthew

And since they broaden their phylacteries beyond measure and make large fringes, courting glory from men, they are rebuked in the rest for seeking the first places at table at dinners and the first chairs in the synagogues, and for pursuing gluttony and glory in public, and for being called rabbi by men, which in the Latin tongue means master. In short, there follows:
On the Veiling of Virgins

So, too, righteousness-for the God of righteousness and of creation is the same-was first in a rudimentary state, having a natural fear of God: from that stage it advanced, through the Law and the Prophets, to infancy; from that stage it passed, through the Gospel, to the fervour of youth: now, through the Paraclete, it is settling into maturity. He will be, after Christ, the only one to be called and revered as Master; for He speaks not from Himself, but what is commanded by Christ.
On Monogamy

Therefore a wife, when her husband is dead, will not marry; for if she marry, she will of course be marrying (his) brother: for "all we are brethren." Again, the woman, if intending to marry, has to marry "in the Lord; " that is, not to an heathen, but to a brother, inasmuch as even the ancient law forbids marriage with members of another tribe.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

The other things then He carried no further than to accuse them, as being small and trifling, and as though His disciples needed not at all to be corrected about these matters; but what was a cause of all the evils, even ambition, and the violent seizing of the teacher's chair, this He brings forward, and corrects with diligence, touching this vehemently and earnestly charging them.

For what saith He? "But be not ye called Rabbi." Then follows the cause also; "For one is your master, and all ye are brethren;" and one hath nothing more than another, in respect of his knowing nothing from himself. Wherefore Paul also saith, "For who is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers?" He said not masters.
Commentary on Matthew

But do not you be called rabbi, for one is your master; and do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven; nor be called masters, because your master is one, Christ. Neither master nor father is anyone else to be called except God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ: Father, because from him are all things; master, because through him are all things, or because through the dispensation of the flesh we have all been reconciled to God. It is asked why, against this precept, the Apostle said that he was the teacher of the Gentiles, or how, in common speech, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and of Egypt, they call one another fathers. This is solved thus: it is one thing to be a father or a master by nature, another by indulgence. If we call a man father, we pay honor to his age; we do not show him to be the author of our life. A master too is so called from fellowship with the true Master. And, not to unfold endless matters: just as one God by nature and one Son does not prejudice others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so also one Father and Master does not prejudice others from being called fathers and masters in a looser sense.
On Repentance

Why not? He had found the son whom he had lost; he had felt him to be all the dearer of whom he had made a gain. Who is that father to be understood by us to be? God, surely: no one is so truly a Father; no one so rich in paternal love.
On Prayer

However, our Lord very frequently proclaimed God as a Father to us; nay, even gave a precept "that we call no one on earth father, but the Father whom we have in the heavens: and so, in thus praying, we are likewise obeying the precept.
On Monogamy
To Abraham, in fine, they appeal; prohibited though they are to acknowledge any other father than God. Grant, now, that Abraham is our father; grant, too, that Paul is.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 50

Seest thou not those who adopt to themselves sons here, how they commit not the act to slaves, but are themselves present at the judgment-seat? Even so neither hath God committed His gift to angels, but Himself is present, commanding and saying, "Call no man Father on earth;" not that thou shouldest dishonor them that gave thee birth, but that thou shouldest prefer to all those Him that made thee, and enrolled thee amongst His own children. For He that hath given the greater, that is, hath set Himself before thee, much more will He not think scorn to distribute unto thee of His body.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

And again, "Call not, father," not that they should not call, but they may know whom they ought to call Father, in the highest sense. For like as the master is not a master principally; so neither is the father. For He is cause of all, both of the masters, and of the fathers.
Commentary on Galatians

But since Abba means Father in the Hebrew and Syriac tongue, and our Lord in the Gospel commands that no one is to be called father except God (Matt. 23), I do not know by what license in the monasteries we either call others by this name or consent to be called by it ourselves. And certainly he gave this command who had said that one must not swear (Matt. 5). If we do not swear, let us not name anyone father either. If we interpret the saying about a father otherwise, we shall be compelled to think otherwise about swearing as well.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

And again He adds, "Neither be ye called guides, for one is your guide, even Christ;" and He said not, I. For like as above He said, "What think ye of Christ?" and He said not, "of me," so here too.

But I should be glad to ask here, what they would say, who are repeatedly applying the term one, one, to the Father alone, to the rejection of the Only-begotten. Is the Father guide? All would declare it, and none would gainsay it. And yet "one," He saith, "is your guide, even Christ." For like as Christ, being called the one guide, casts not out the Father from being guide; even so the Father, being called Master, doth not cast out the Son from being Master. For the expression, one, one, is spoken in contra-distinction to men, and the rest of the creation.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 72

Having warned them therefore against this grievous pest, and amended them, He instructs also how they may escape it; by humility. Wherefore He adds also, "He that is greatest among you shall be your servant. For whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased, and whosoever shall abase himself shall be exalted."

For nothing is equal to the practice of modesty, wherefore He is continually reminding them of this virtue, both when He brought the children into the midst, and now. And, when on the mount, beginning the beatitudes, He began from hence. And in this place, He plucks it up by the roots hereby, saying, "He that abaseth himself shall be exalted."

Seest thou how He draws off the hearer right over to the contrary thing. For not only doth He forbid him to set his heart upon the first place, but requires him to follow after the last. For so shalt thou obtain thy desire, He saith. Wherefore he that pursues his desire for the first, must follow after the last place. "For he that abaseth himself shall be exalted."
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 13

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter.

Those who dare to call God not good on account of the curses which God set down against sinners in his law — let them hear how, as truly the Son of that God who gave the law, in likeness indeed of the blessings which are set down in the law, he too pronounces the beatitudes of those who are saved, but in likeness of the curses set down in the law he sets woe against sinners, saying: woe to you and to you. And let those who bring a charge against the God of the law, hearing these things, not understanding that those things too were spoken by a kindly God, say what we ought to understand concerning Jesus when he says: woe to you, scribes and Pharisees. Those who confess that it belongs to goodness to pronounce such things against sinners — let them understand that the purpose of God is the same in bringing forth the curses of the law within the law. But whether it be that curse or this pronounced woe — it befalls each sinner not from the pronouncement of the one pronouncing, but from the sins of the sinner himself, who offers himself worthy for the reception either of those curses or of these woes, which God pronounced for the sake of discipline against those men, that he might turn them to the good. For a father too, rebuking his son, frequently brings forth for his amendment certain words which seem to be curses, and yet he does not wish him to become worthy of those curses, but rather desires to turn him away from them.

We have said these things in order to show that the Gospels are in agreement with the law. So too now, when he says woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you shut the kingdom of heaven, he terrified the scribes and Pharisees, that they might not mock the kingdom of heaven before men. But the scribes and Pharisees shutting the kingdom of heaven offend in two ways at once: in one indeed that they themselves do not enter into the kingdom of heaven, and secondly that those entering they do not allow to enter. These two sins are by nature inseparable from one another. For whoever sins in one of these cannot abstain from the other. Likewise, conversely, whoever abstains from the one, it is impossible that he should not also abstain from the other; for instance, no one is found who, himself entering into the kingdom of heaven, does not permit others to enter, since for him who forbids others to enter into the kingdom this very thing — that he does not permit others to enter — suffices for his own expulsion, so that he does not enter into the kingdom of heaven; for whoever "shall scandalize one of the little ones" of the Church, forbidding anyone to enter into the kingdom of heaven, will suffer what is written in the Gospel, woe. Likewise, conversely, whoever is able to make someone enter into the kingdom of heaven — if indeed it is within his power both to permit and to forbid — much more will he himself enter into the kingdom of heaven.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 14

Since the Lord frequently says woe to the scribes and Pharisees, we will set out the cause of each woe in its proper place. But now let us set out the cause of this present woe. The cause, then, of the present woe is that they were shutting up the kingdom of heaven before men; and in shutting it before others, they themselves did not enter, precisely because they forbade to enter those who would surely have entered, if they had not been shut out by these men. And first, indeed, the present passage is to be expounded simply, as of the scribes and Pharisees who are found among the Jews. For these men, not content that they themselves did not believe the Lord, went still further and disparaged his teaching and overthrew every prophecy written concerning him and blasphemed his every work as false and feigned by the devil, saying, "this man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul", and showed themselves murderous toward those who had believed in Christ, and in every way forbade anyone to come to Christianity, through which one enters into the kingdom of heaven. They were shutting up that which had been openly announced and preached in the sight of all and proclaimed aloud among all men. And in shutting up the kingdom of heaven they themselves did not enter (for neither did they wish to hear him who said: "if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved, and shall go in and go out and find pasture"); and those entering (that is, those who could believe on account of the faith which "from the law and the prophets" had earlier been declared concerning Christ) they did not permit to enter. Utterly breaking up the very beginning of their assent, and with all terror and savage boldness, as far as lay in them, they themselves, by shutting the door, forbade all who wished to enter through the door.

To this simple exposition we will join also this, concerning those who sin among us. For all who by an evil manner of life urge on an example of sinning among the people, and who do injury to those who are still little ones in Christ and imperfect, disheartening and scandalizing them, seem to shut the kingdom of heaven before men, and neither do they themselves enter nor do they permit others to enter. And this sin is found indeed even among the common people, but most of all among the teachers, who indeed teach men according to the justice of the Gospel, but do not do what they teach, because they are evil shepherds and therefore do not spare the sheep nor care for their salvation, but always look to the gains coming to them from men in return for the fact that they seem to feed the people when they do not feed them, and are caught in filthy gains and in the lusts of empty glory. For these are the wages of the hirelings, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men and do not enter into it, nor do they wish to understand what is said: "strive to enter through the narrow door". And since above all contests this is the contest, that one should be doing violence and seizing the heavenly kingdom, to such teachers, then, these words are fittingly said, neither do you enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter, especially if we see them, by their evil life and pride and revilings and avarice, leading into scandal not, I will say, one of the little ones, but even, as far as lies in them, all. Woe, then, to those who shut the kingdom of heaven before men, either in this way or in another; but blessed are those who open it either by their word or by their good work, like him who said: "a great and evident door has been opened to me", or as the rest of the apostles opened it. And if anyone becomes an imitator of them, he opens the kingdom of heaven before men by his justice and virtue and chastity and wisdom. And the more one advances in piety, the more he opens the kingdom of heaven before men.

I think, therefore, that all who profess that they enter into the church, altogether either shut the kingdom of heaven before men by their evil manners of life insofar as they themselves sin, or open it by their good acts insofar as they have conducted themselves justly. Most of all do this those who seem to be more illustrious in the church, such as bishops, presbyters, deacons. For by living well and teaching well the word of truth they open the kingdom of heaven before men and, while they themselves enter, they provoke others to enter; but the evil ones, who are not shepherds but hirelings, shut the kingdom of heaven before men and do not hear what the Apostle says: "but we endure all things, that we may give no offense to the Gospel of Christ". Indeed one may see many teachers not permitting to enter into the kingdom of heaven those who desire to enter — especially when, without judgment and without reason, not on account of the sins which they commit, they excommunicate certain persons, but on account of some jealousy and contentiousness they frequently forbid to enter even those who are better than they themselves are. And they indeed are not permitted to enter, but those others, who are sober in mind and watchful in spirit, overcoming by their patience and long-suffering the tyrannies of these men, though forbidden nevertheless enter and inherit the kingdom of heaven.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 15

Next let us see whether, beyond those we have spoken of, it is possible to see also others who shut and open the kingdom of heaven. For those who have been counted worthy and fit to expound the Gospel, and who show themselves such that they can truly say "Do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?", open the kingdom of heaven before men, when they demonstrate, with all clarity and proof, the loftiness of the divine words — words which were not spoken about earthly things but about heaven and about the mind of the Lord, who came to men — so that, so far as it lies in them, they would lead "Gentiles and barbarians, wise and unwise" to the piety of Christ. But those who, through their unteachableness and unrighteousness, with much rashness gave themselves over to the profession of teaching before they had learned and come to know the truth, and who therefore, in imitation of vain Jewish fables, hand down the bodily narratives of the Scriptures and not their spiritual sense or intention, and who moreover disparage those "who have risen with Christ and seek the things that are above" in the Scriptures "and not upon the earth," nor reckon that the truth set forth in the Scriptures lies in earthly things: these, so far as it lies in them, shut the kingdom of heaven before men, shutting it by their unrighteousness and drawing to themselves those who were able — by hearing the more divine and greater teaching and the loftiness of the truth — to enter into the kingdom of heaven through the heavenly doctrines and through the deeds befitting them. To this exposition it is fitting what Luke writes: "Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves have not entered in, and you have hindered those who were entering." For those who accuse the allegorical exposition and want to teach that the divine Scripture is plain and has nothing more than the text shows, and who do not admit any more divine sense concerning circumcision or the Passover or the unleavened bread or foods and drinks or the feasts or the new moons or the sabbaths, and do not accept that the Jews then served "in the display and shadow of things to come" — these indeed are lawyers, yet they have taken away "the key of knowledge," so far as their teaching goes, that is, taking away every way of the law for understanding its ordinances; and therefore neither did they themselves enter in nor, so far as it lay in them, did they permit others to enter.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

"Woe unto you, for ye shut up the kingdom against men; for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in." But if to profit no one be a charge against a man, even to hurt and hinder, what plea hath that? But what means, "them that are entering in?" Them that are fit for it. For when they were to lay injunctions on others, they used to make the burdens intolerable, but when they themselves were to do any of the things required, on the contrary, so far from doing anything, they went much beyond this in wickedness, they even used to corrupt others. These are they that are called pests, who make their employment the ruin of others, standing right contrary to teachers. For if it be the part of a teacher to save that which is perishing, to destroy that which is on the point of being saved is that of a destroyer.
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men; you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter. The scribes and Pharisees have knowledge of the law and the prophets; they know that Christ is the Son of God; they are not ignorant that he was born of a virgin; but while they seek plunder from the common people subject to them, they neither enter the kingdoms of heaven themselves nor permit those who could enter. This is what he rebukes in the prophet Hosea: The priests have hidden the way, they have killed Shechem; and again: The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? Or else every teacher who causes his disciples to stumble by evil works shuts the kingdom of heaven before them.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

"Woe unto you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretense make long prayers: therefore ye shall receive greater damnation."

After this, next He derides them for gluttony: and the grievous thing was, that not from rich men's goods, but from the poor they indulged their own belly, and aggravated their poverty, which they should have relieved. For neither did they merely eat, but devoured.

Moreover also the manner of their overreaching was yet more grievous, "for a pretense making long prayers."

For every one is worthy of vengeance who doeth any evil thing; but he that is deriving even the reason for so doing from godliness, and is using this cloke for his wickedness, is justly liable to a far more grievous punishment. And wherefore did He not depose them? Because the time suffered it not as yet. So therefore He lets them alone for a time, but by His sayings, He secures that the people be not deceived, lest, through the dignity of those men, they be drawn on to the same emulation.

For as He had said, "Whatsoever they bid you do, that do;" He shows how many things they do amiss, lest from thence He should be supposed amongst the unwise to commit all to them.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 16

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who go about the sea and the dry land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a son of gehenna twice as much as you yourselves are.

These things are fittingly said, after the coming of Christ, to the scribes and Pharisees of Jewish words, who diligently go about very many places of the world in order to persuade newcomers to Judaize. For whoever Judaize after the Savior are taught to imitate the disposition of those who said at that time: "Crucify, crucify him", and again "Away with such a one from the earth"; and they are taught also to accuse him, just as then the priests of the people used to accuse him. And it is possible to see them even now, when a robber is being judged and a Christian bears witness to the truth, wishing rather that the imitator of Barabbas be acquitted than the disciple of Christ. All of which things make the proselyte a son of gehenna not simply, but, as it is written, twofold beyond the scribes and Pharisees who made him a proselyte.

But someone will say in this place: how is the disciple, a proselyte to those who are now the wretchedly constituted scribes and Pharisees, not made a son of gehenna equally with his teachers, but twofold? For he will say that he ought to become a son of gehenna less, and, if anything, by half, than the one who made him a proselyte. Or, if one should even grant that the disciple be "as his master", the disciple ought to become a son of gehenna equally with his master. I think, therefore, that every man who from the Gentile manner of life has been made a proselyte of the Jews was a son of gehenna even before he becomes a proselyte. For a life subjected to idolatries is sufficient of itself to make a man a son of gehenna. Such a son of gehenna, therefore, the word of our Lord Jesus Christ does indeed save and set free through the "washing of baptism", giving him the power to become a son of God and showing him the way, so that he may become a son of God the Father who is in heaven. But the word of the Jews who do not believe in Christ not only does not release the Gentile from gehenna, but still adds to him a further count of damnation, so that according to Judaism too he becomes a son of gehenna. And thus the scribe or Pharisee makes another a son of gehenna more than himself, not because he himself makes him twofold, but because, when the man has been made …, he is made twofold a son of gehenna through the teaching of his teacher. And thus the one who taught becomes the cause of that man's second error, so that he becomes twofold a son of gehenna above the one who taught him ill. But another will say in another way, that those who from the beginning were nurtured in the law of Moses are already sons of gehenna, because they did not believe in Christ. But those who have left the Gentile life, once judging to abandon the idolatry in which they had been nurtured, and have taken hold of the Jewish life, are worthy of a double punishment, because they did not abandon it with inquiry, nor were they willing to examine the Jewish word and that which seems to be akin to the Jewish word, that is, the profession of Christians, nor did they investigate through those who are competent to teach both sects, so that they might understand which word was the truer and rather to be chosen. At the same time we learn from this place that among those also who are to be in gehenna there will be a difference of torments, since the one is simply a son of gehenna, while the other is twofold.

But this too we must consider: whether someone becomes a son of gehenna still more abundantly, for instance threefold or manifold according to the multitude of his sins; and whether it is generally the case that someone becomes a son of gehenna, for instance a Jew or a Gentile or the professor of any false doctrine whatsoever, or also specially, so that through the individual kinds of sins one becomes a son of gehenna: for instance, he who fornicates becomes a son of gehenna, but he who also commits adultery becomes so twofold, while he who also commits theft becomes so still threefold (according to what is written: "with what measure you have measured, with the same measure it shall be measured to you"), so that the righteous man indeed is increased in glory according to the number of his righteous deeds, but the sinner is multiplied in gehenna according to the number of his sins. But what this gehenna is, and in what place of the scriptures it was first named, let him who is able inquire, especially in the division of the inheritance of Joshua the son of Nun, where sometimes it is called the valley of the son of Hinnom, but sometimes the valley of Hinnom, which is Gehenna (for Ge is a VALLEY), and let him observe that, just as Jerusalem is the portion of the tribe of Benjamin and certain other chosen cities or villages, so also is Gehenna. And it is consequent for him who knows what Jerusalem is in the division of the true inheritance of the sons of Israel, that he should understand the discourse about gehenna. But he who reads Joshua the son of Nun diligently, let him see also which villages are there reported to neighbor the valley that is called Gehenna. It has seemed to me not to be safe to hand these things down at greater length and more openly through ink and pen and paper; would that these very things which we do say may not seem to have been said rashly and perilously!
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

After this, again another charge: "Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves;" that is, not even the fact that hardly ye have taken him, and with endless toils, induces you to be sparing towards him, although of the things we have hardly acquired, we are more sparing, but you not even this renders more gentle.

Here He lays to their charge two things; one, that they are unprofitable for the salvation of the many, and need much toil in order to win over even one; another, that they were remiss in the preservation of him whom they had gained, or rather that they were not only careless, but even traitors, by their wickedness in their life corrupting him, and making him worse. For when the disciple sees his teachers to be such as these, he becomes worse than they. For he stops not at his teacher's wickedness; but as when his teacher is virtuous, he imitates him, so when he is bad, he even goes beyond him, by reason of our proneness to what is evil.

And He calls him "a child of hell," that is, a very hell. And He said "twofold more than you," that He might both alarm those, and make these feel the more severely, because they are teachers of wickedness. And not this only, but because they labor to instill into their disciples a greater wickedness, hardening them to a much greater depravity than they have, and this is above all a mark of a depraved soul.
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you go around sea and dry land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves. We do not keep what we have sought with the same zeal with which we seek it. The scribes and Pharisees, traversing the whole world for the sake of trade and various gains, to be captured as much from their disciples as through a show of holiness, made it their zeal to make a proselyte from the Gentiles, that is, to mingle a stranger, an uncircumcised man, with the people of God. But he who before, while he was a heathen, went astray in simplicity and was a son of Gehenna once, seeing the vices of his teachers and understanding that they destroy by deed what they taught by words, returns to his vomit and, having become a Gentile, will be worthy of greater punishment as a transgressor. He is called a son of Gehenna in the way one is called a son of perdition and a son of this world. For each one is called the son of him whose works he does.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 17

Woe to you, guides of the blind, who say: whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it, is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift? He therefore who swears by the altar swears by it and by all things that are upon it. And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. And he who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it.

By this saying too he censures the traditions of the Pharisees, as being not upright. He does this also in that passage where he reproaches the traditions of the Pharisees made against the commandment of God, which had been laid down concerning the honor of father or mother, when the Pharisees said: "whoever shall say to his father or mother: a gift, whatever from me may profit you, he shall not honor his father". After which he adds and says: "you have made void the commandment of God, that you may establish your own tradition", and he brings forward the example of Isaiah, saying: "this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; and in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men". One, then, of the Pharisaic traditions was such, concerning those who swear, since some indeed swore by the temple, but others by the gold of the temple, likewise others by the altar, others by the gift of the altar; and they said that he was a debtor who swore by the gold of the temple or by the gift of the altar, but that he was in no respect liable who swore by the temple or by the altar.

Therefore, speaking against traditions of this kind to the Jews, and wishing to correct them from human traditions to the divine commandments, the Savior says that they are blind and foolish who hand down such things, not seeing that everything which is placed in the temple is not sanctified through itself, but through the temple. So too what is placed upon the altar is judged to be already God's gift from the fact that it has been received upon the altar. If, then, the cause of sanctifying the gold is the temple, and of sanctifying the gift the altar, how would it not seem foolish that the one who swears by that which sanctifies is not guilty, while the one who swears by that which is sanctified seems to be guilty, as though that which is sanctified were better than that which sanctifies? So, since the Jews have the custom of swearing also by heaven, to the foregoing he added this too for the reproof of those who swore more readily by heaven than by God, since he acts equally irrationally who swears by heaven, just as he who swears by the temple or by the altar; for he who swears by heaven is seen also to swear by him who sits upon it, and does not (as he supposes) escape the danger from the fact that he swears not by God himself, but by the throne of God. And these things he says to the Jews, forbidding men to give heed to the traditions of the Pharisees. For otherwise, above, he plainly forbade to swear "at all".
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 18

But if it is necessary to bring somewhat more deeply to light, at least in part, the meaning of Scripture that lies hidden as it were in such fields of the Gospel and is not comprehensible to just anyone, it must be said: every oath is a binding and a confirmation of the word about which one swears. Therefore an oath is to be understood as every testimony of the Scriptures that is brought forward for the confirmation and binding of our word which we speak, so that "all Scripture divinely inspired" is indeed the temple of the glory of God, and the meaning placed within it is the gold. Therefore, in support of all the words that we bring forward in teaching, we ought to bring forward the meaning of Scripture as though confirming the meaning that we set forth. For just as all gold that is outside the temple is not sanctified, so every meaning that is outside the divine Scripture (however admirable it may seem to some) is not holy, because it is not contained by the meaning of Scripture, which is accustomed to sanctify only that meaning which it has within itself, as the temple sanctifies its own proper gold. We ought not, therefore, in order to confirm our teaching, to swear by our own private understandings and take them as testimonies, those things which each one of us understands and reckons to be according to truth, unless he has shown them to be holy, from the fact that they are contained in the divine Scriptures as though in certain temples of God. Fools therefore and blind are all those who do not recognize that the temple, that is, the reading of the Scriptures, makes a meaning great and venerable, as it does the consecrated gold.

But consider further whether perhaps, according to the likeness of the temple and the gold placed in the temple, we ought to understand the altar and the gift which is placed upon the altar. The altar, then, which sanctifies the offering, is the heart of man, which is held to be the principal thing in man; and the offerings and gifts which are placed upon the altar are everything that is placed upon the heart. For instance, you propose to pray: you have placed the offering of prayer upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer prayer to God. You have proposed to sing psalms: you have placed the offering of psalms upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer to God the offering of psalms. You have proposed to give alms: you have placed the offering of almsgiving upon your heart, as upon a certain altar, in order to offer the offering of almsgiving to God. You have proposed to fast: you have placed the offering of fasting upon your heart, as upon a certain altar …. Therefore the heart of man, from which the offering is offered to God, makes every offering venerable and holy. For this reason the offering cannot be more honorable than the heart of man, from which the offering is transmitted. Blind, therefore, is every man who sees either someone's great almsgivings or psalms or great prayers or fastings, and without judgment pronounces them blessed, and does not consider from what sort of heart the almsgivings are offered, or the psalms, or the prayers, or the fastings. For the altar is the heart which sanctifies the offering of him who is pure of heart. For if the heart and conscience of a man "does not prick him, he has confidence toward God". Not on account of his gifts, nor the words of prayer or psalm, however well composed they may seem and selected from the Scriptures, but because (so to speak) he has well built the altar of his heart. He, therefore, who takes the altar, that is, the principal heart and the conscience, as witness, swears by the altar, embracing everything that is contained in it. And he who swears, according to what we have handed down, by the temple, that is by Scripture, is seen to swear by Scripture and by the word and meaning of God which is contained in it.

But there is a third point, that we may say that above the temple, that is, above all Scripture, and above the altar, that is, above every heart, there is a certain understanding above the understanding of all the Scriptures and above every heart, "which has not yet ascended into the heart of man", which morally is called heaven, a throne now not "of the glory of God", as the temple is, but of God himself. For the temple is the temple of the glory of God, in which "we see through a mirror in an enigma"; but heaven, which is above the temple of God himself, in which is the throne of God, in which it is possible to behold "with unveiled face", "when that which is perfect shall have come", the face of the mysteries of the truth that sit in a heaven of this kind.
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound. Fools and blind, for which is greater: the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound. Blind ones, for which is greater: the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? He, therefore, who swears by the altar swears by it and by all things that are upon it; and he who swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it; and he who swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. Above, as seemed good to us, we explained what was signified by the tradition of the Pharisees who said: Whatever gift is from me will profit you. Now a tradition of the Pharisees is condemned that is double and draws toward the one occasion of avarice, so that they are convicted of doing all for gain and not for the fear of God. For as, in the broadened phylacteries and fringes, the reputation for holiness courted glory, and through the occasion of glory sought gain, so another scheme devised by their tradition convicts the teachers of impiety. If anyone, in a dispute or in some quarrel or in a doubtful case, had sworn by the temple and was afterwards convicted of a lie, he was not held guilty of the crime; but if he had sworn by the gold and the money that was offered to the priests in the temple, he was at once compelled to pay that by which he had sworn. Again, if anyone had sworn by the altar, no one held him guilty of perjury; but if he had perjured himself by the gift or by the offerings, that is, by the sacrifice or by the victims, by fine flour and the other things that are offered to God upon the altar, these they demanded back most zealously. The Lord therefore convicts them both of folly and of fraud, because the temple is much greater than the gold which is sanctified by the temple, and the altar than the sacrifices which are sanctified by the altar. And they did all this not out of the fear of God but out of desire for riches.
On Prayer

His hands, at all events, are ever unclean, eternally dyed with the blood of the prophets, and of the Lord Himself; and on that account, as being hereditary culprits from their privity to their fathers' crimes, they do not dare even to raise them unto the Lord, for fear some Isaiah should cry out, for fear Christ should utterly shudder.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 19

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and you have left behind the weightier things of the law, judgment and mercy and faith; but these things it was necessary to do, and not to omit those. Blind guides, straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel (23, 23. 24).

This word must be spoken at a fitting time to those who indeed display religion toward God in the smallest matters, but in matters great and necessary hold in contempt the commandment and God himself who commanded them. Such things happened even among the Jews, who supposed themselves to be keeping the law of Moses, who prescribed that from all fruits tithes be given to the Levites and the priests. And so, since it was easy to fulfill the law in the smallest matters, they tithed indeed mint and dill and cumin, and all (so to speak) the smallest things and those that were light in the law, but its weighty things they did not observe, that is, judgment and mercy and faith: judgment indeed, that each one should judge concerning all things with a just judgment and not concerning only some, and should assent to him who said: "I desire mercy, rather than sacrifice", so that he might offer to God the sacrifices of acts of mercy, so that, examining those things which are of faith, he might be faithful. But since it was fitting that certain of those hearing the Lord speak these things about tithing the smallest matters might come to despise the tithing of the smallest things, the Lord wisely added, saying: and these it was necessary to do (that is, judgment and mercy and faith) and not to omit those (that is, the tithing of mint and dill and cumin). And he says that those who do such things, the scribes and Pharisees, who omit the weightier things of the law and tithe the contemptible things among the fruits, are blind guides. And he wisely says that such men strain out (that is, expel from themselves) the smallest faults, which he named gnats, but "swallow" (that is, commit) the greatest faults, which he named camels, animals evidently twisted and huge. According to these words, therefore, every man who omits the weightier things of the law (especially judgment and mercy and faith) swallows a camel. And not only among the Jews, but also among us, one may find many sinning sins of this kind and swallowing camels, in that they commit the greatest faults; and one may frequently observe men of this kind, how in the smallest matters they display their religion. And he rightly calls them hypocrites; for wishing to acquire religiosity "before men", they are unwilling to take up that religiosity which God has justified. We must therefore flee such pretenses of the scribes and Pharisees, lest that woe befall us also, just as it befell them.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 20

But I judge that, morally, all are called scribes who suppose nothing more to be set down in the Scriptures than what the plain wording of the Scripture shows, but who moreover despise those who "search out the depth of God". Likewise all are Pharisees who justify themselves and separate themselves from the rest, "saying: Do not draw near to me, for I am clean". Now the Pharisees are interpreted, according to the name Phares, as THE DIVIDED, who divided themselves from the rest; for Phares in the Hebrew tongue means DIVISION. But if in words of the Gospel of this kind one must also take up a moral understanding, it must be known that, just as mint and dill and cumin are seasonings of foods and not themselves the principal foods, so in our ways of life there are certain things that are indeed principal and necessary for the justification of our souls — such as these weightier matters of the law, judgment and mercy and faith — but others that are, as it were, seasonings of our acts, commending them and making them more pleasant, such as abstaining from laughter and fasting, the bending of the knees, perseverance in the assemblies, assiduity in the communion, and other things like these, which are not themselves the justices, but are held to be the seasonings of the justices. But the spiritual things that are justices of themselves are called judgment and mercy and faith. It is disgraceful, therefore, to observe these least things (which is to tithe), yet not to offer to God the observances of the necessary things (that is, not to tithe). And those who do and teach these things, like the former ones, are blind guides. And how should they not be reckoned blind, from whom the greatness and the twistedness of camels — that is, of perverse acts — lies hidden, and who do not see that it profits nothing to strain out and to be scrupulous as an examiner in the least matters, while the principal things and those that truly pertain to the glory of God are neglected? Since, therefore, there are many even among us who suppose they are living carefully with regard to trivial matters, but with regard to the necessary matters despise themselves, the present discourse confounds men of this sort — not indeed forbidding them to observe those trivial things, but commanding them to guard more carefully the principal and more salutary things. He, therefore, strains out all things who, in all things whatsoever he does or speaks or thinks, separates what is sordid and earthly and not adorned with divine reasonings from those things that are by nature bright and sincere and just, according to him who teaches: "let us keep the feast not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth". But you will find many who are reckoned to believe, yet do not have their words and acts and thoughts strained out. Therefore "as hay" shall "the fire consume" their carnal acts, torturing the soul also together with the body on account of the bodily faults grown fast to it. For just as it is not possible to cut away the superfluities grown upon bodies without great pain and torment for those who suffer them, so neither the carnal deeds from those who (so to speak) have made their souls flesh; wherefore it was said concerning such souls: "my spirit shall not remain in these men, for they are flesh".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

Then He derides them for folly also, because they bade them disregard the greater commandments. And yet before He had said the opposite, that "they bind heavy burdens, and grievous to be borne." But these things too they did again and were doing everything for the corruption of those who were subject to them, in little things requiring strictness, and despising the great.

"For ye pay tithe," He saith, "of mint and anise, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, and mercy, and faith. These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone."

Here then He naturally saith it, where it is tithe and almsgiving, for what doth it hurt to give alms? But not to keep the law; for neither doth it say thus. Therefore here indeed He saith, "These ought ye to have done;" but where He is speaking about clean and unclean, He no longer adds this, but makes a distinction, and shows that the inward purity is necessarily followed by the outward, but the converse is no longer so.

For where there is a plea of love to man, He passes it over lightly, for this very reason, and because it was not yet time expressly and plainly to revoke the things of the law. But where it is an observance of bodily purification, He overthrows it more plainly.

Then, to show that there is no harm arising from despising bodily cleansings, but very great vengeance from not regarding the purifications of the soul, which is virtue, He called these "a gnat," for they are small and nothing, but those other a camel, for they were beyond what men could bear. Wherefore also He saith, "Straining at the gnat, and swallowing the camel." For indeed the one were enacted for the sake of the other, I mean of mercy and judgment; so that not even then did they profit being done alone. For whereas the little things were mentioned for the sake of the great, and after that these last were neglected, and labor was spent on those alone, nothing was gained even then by this. For the greater followed not the lesser, but the lesser were sure to follow these greater.

But these things He saith to show, that even before grace was come, these were not among the principal things, or amongst those upon which men should spend their labor, but the matters required were different. But if before the grace they were so, much more when high commandments had come, were these things unprofitable, and it was not meet to practise them at all.

In every case then is vice a grievous thing, but especially when it does not so much as think it needs amendment; and it is yet more grievous, when it thinks itself sufficient even to amend others; to express which Christ calls them "blind guides." For if for a blind man not to think he needs a guide be extreme misery and wretchedness; when he wishes himself to guide others, see to what a gulf it leads.

But these things He said, by all intimating their mad desire of glory, and their exceeding frenzy concerning this pest. For this became a cause to them of all their evils, namely, that they did all things for display. This both led them away from the faith, and caused them to neglect what really is virtue, and induced them to busy themselves about bodily purifyings only, neglecting the purifications of the soul. So therefore to lead them into what really is virtue, and to the purifyings of the soul, He makes mention of mercy, and judgment, and faith. For these are the things that comprise our life, these are what purify the soul, justice, love to man, truth; the one inclining us to pardon and not suffering us to be excessively severe and unforgiving to them that sin (for then shall we gain doubly, both becoming kind to man, and hence meeting also ourselves with much kindness from the God of all), and causing us both to sympathize with them that are despitefully entreated, and to assist them; the other not suffering them to be deceitful, and crafty.

But neither when He saith, "These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone," doth He say it as introducing a legal observance; away with the thought; neither with regard to the platter and the cup, when He said, "Cleanse that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also," doth He bring us unto the old regard for little things, but on the contrary indeed, He doth all things to show it to be superfluous. For He said not, Cleanse the outside of them also, but that which is within, and the outside is sure to follow.
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin and have left aside the weightier things of the law, judgment and mercy and faith; these you ought to have done, and not to omit those. There are many precepts in the law which display types of things to come, but others which are plain, according to the psalmist who says: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes, which demand works at once, for example: You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, and the rest. But the Pharisees, because the Lord had commanded (to leave aside the mystical senses for the moment) that, for the support of the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord, tithes of all things be offered in the temple, had this one zeal: that what had been ordered should be brought in; the other things, which were greater, whether anyone did them or not, they counted of little worth. And so from this passage too he convicts them of avarice, because they zealously exact tithes even of cheap herbs, and pass over judgment in the settling of business, and mercy toward the poor, orphans and widows, and faith in God, which are great things.
Commentary on Matthew

Blind guides, straining out the gnat, but swallowing the camel. By the camel I think is meant, according to the sense of the present passage, the greatness of the precepts, judgment and mercy and faith; and by the gnat the tithes of mint and dill and cumin and of the other cheap herbs. These things, which are great, we devour and neglect against the precept of God, and in small things that bring gain we make a show of religion and of diligence.
On Prayer

But what reason is there in going to prayer with hands indeed washed, but the spirit foul?-inasmuch as to our hands themselves spiritual purities are necessary, that they may be "lifted up pure" from falsehood, from murder, from cruelty, from poisonings, from idolatry, and all the other blemishes which, conceived by the spirit, are effected by the operation of the hands. These are the true purities; not those which most are superstitiously careful about, taking water at every prayer, even when they are coming from a bath of the whole body.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 21

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean what is outside of the cup and the dish, but within you are full of plunder and intemperance and deceit. Blind Pharisee, clean first what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may become clean (23, 25, 26).

This saying instructs us to be eager to be just, not to appear just. For whoever is intent on appearing just cleans the things that are outside and attends to what is seen, but neglects his own heart and conscience — not considering that the one who is intent on the things that are within and is eager to clean his own thoughts, consequently is also eager to make clean the things that are outside. But if anyone is eager for the things that are seen and yet neglects the interior things of his soul, it is necessary that such a man be filled from within with avarice, wantonness, malice, and very many other evils. For everyone who is anxious about his own salvation (which is from within) is also anxious about his reputation (which is from outside); but not everyone who is anxious about his reputation from outside is also anxious about his own salvation from within. For example, it is written: "whoever looks at a woman to desire her has committed adultery in his heart". This man, then, who abstains from the deed of fornication but fornicates in the desire of his heart, has cleaned what is outside of the cup and the dish or the platter, but is within full of intemperance. But also the one who gives alms in order to obtain glory from men seems indeed to clean what is outside of the cup and the dish, giving alms "before men", but is within full of the lust for empty glory and intemperance. And whatever good a man does not from a clean conscience for the sake of God, he seems indeed clean on the outside, but on the inside he is full of evils. But also all the professors of false doctrine are cups cleaned as it were on the outside because of the appearance of religion which they feign, but within they are full of plunder and seduction, by which they carry off men into error. And they are "ravenous wolves" lurking under "sheep's clothing" and devouring simple souls, who are not able to see that they are ravenous wolves because of the covering of the sheep's skins.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 22

But if we must consider everything in the Gospel discourses morally, we must see why in Matthew the scribes and Pharisees are said to cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, whereas in Luke mention is made of the cup and the platter. Both, then, set down vessels of food and drink; and both name the cup (which is for drinking), but not both the dish: the one names the platter, the other the dish (yet each is held to be a vessel for food). Therefore, according to each evangelist, there is a certain spiritual drink and spiritual food, which we take in the discourses of the Scriptures of the Law or of the Prophets. And so every discourse by which we are given spiritual drink, or every narrative by which we are nourished, are vessels of drink and of food. We are admonished, therefore, not to have care for the discourses or narratives that are on the outside, but for those that are within, so that our heart may be filled with pure senses of drink and of nourishment, and not with words nor with their ornate compositions — because "the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power". For instance, one who is eager to bring forth a polished discourse in words rather than one filled with saving sense, the cup of his narrative is cleansed on the outside, but within it is filled with the filth of vanity. Hence Paul, who was not accustomed to cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish but the inside, confesses himself unskilled "in speech but not in knowledge"; and his speech was indeed rustic, yet clean because of the cleanness of its knowledge. But those who spoke "in the wisdom of word" and through this made void the cross of Christ, presented their discourses clean indeed on the outside, but within full of unclean knowledge, and of plunder and intemperance of life. Likewise, whoever, hearing the word or some Scripture of the Law, is delighted by its outward and common compositions rather than by its inner and saving senses, loves the cup or the dish cleansed on the outside, but within filthy.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 23

But if it is also fitting to add a third exposition, kindred to the earlier ones, we say that the letters of the law and the prophets are the cups of spiritual drinks of the soul and the dishes of necessary foods of faithful men, or the bowls of foods wisely seasoned. Of these cups and dishes and bowls of the law or of the prophets, the scribes and Pharisees are indeed eager for the outward and common sense, and they hasten to demonstrate that this is clean and holy; but the disciples of Christ hasten to cleanse and sanctify the inner and spiritual sense by knowledge and by probable demonstration, so that they may eat and drink the law and the prophets cleansed from within, desiring to hear and receive the inner and mystical sense, and passing beyond the outward senses of the words. It is good, therefore, to cleanse carefully from within the cup or the dish or the bowl, because for him who has cleansed first that which is within the cup, those things also which are outside become truly cleansed; and then the vessels of words are found clean, when their true and spiritual senses have been made manifest.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

So, therefore, while with respect to alms He saith, "These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the others undone," touching purifications He speaks not on this wise, but what? "Ye make clean," He saith, "the outside of the cup and the platter, but within they are full of extortion, and injustice. Cleanse that which is within the cup, that the outside may be clean also." And He took it from a thing confessed and manifest, from a cup and platter.

And besides, neither is it concerning a cup and platter he is speaking, but of soul and body, by the outside meaning the body, by the inside the soul. But if with regard to the platter there be need of that which is within much more with regard to thee.

But ye do the contrary, saith He, observing things trifling and external, ye neglect what are great and inward: whence very great mischief arises, for that thinking ye have duly performed all, ye despise the other things; and despising them, ye do not so much as strive or attempt to perform them.
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean what is outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of plunder and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first clean what is inside of the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may become clean. In different words, with the same sense as above, he convicts the Pharisees of pretense and falsehood, because they show one thing to men outside and do another at home; not that their superstition dwelt in the cup and the dish, but that outside they showed men holiness in dress, in speech, in phylacteries, in fringes, in the length of their prayers and in other things of this kind, while inwardly they were full of the filth of vices.
On Repentance
We are not washed in order that we may cease sinning, but because we have ceased, since in heart we have been bathed already.
On the Resurrection of the Flesh

Wherefore that also must be held to be the resurrection, when a man is reanimated by access to the truth, and having dispersed the death of ignorance, and being endowed with new life by God, has burst forth from the sepulchre of the old man, even as the Lord likened the scribes and Pharisees to "whited sepulchres." Whence it follows that they who have by faith attained to the resurrection, are with the Lord after they have once put Him on in their baptism.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 24

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every foulness. So you also outwardly indeed appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity (23, 27. 28).

For just as above "within they are full of plunder and intemperance," so likewise here also they are full of hypocrisy and iniquity, which are compared to the bones of the dead and to every uncleanness. For hypocrisy, since it is a certain pretense of good, has indeed nothing living from that good which it feigns, but has (so to speak) the bone of that virtue which it feigns. … the righteousness or chastity is dead. For if we hear wisely what the present discourse wishes to show, we understand that all feigned righteousness is dead righteousness, or rather is not even righteousness at all. Just as a dead man is indeed seen to be a man but is not a man, so also dead chastity is not chastity either; and it is dead which is done not for the sake of God but in pretense for the sake of men. And just as it is with mimes, who take up the persons of certain others and are not themselves the ones they feign but only seem to be, so he who feigns righteousness — his feigned righteousness is not righteousness but only seems to be; for it is not righteousness, but a figment of righteousness. So also in seduction feigned chastity is not chastity, but only seems to be. On which account men of this kind are well likened to whitened tombs, outwardly indeed appearing beautiful, for they too outwardly are seen to be righteous in the sight of those who do not know how to consider the inner things, but within they are full of the bones of the dead.

There are as many bones in them and uncleannesses as there are good works they feign out of an evil disposition: and outwardly they are seen righteous "before men," not before those whom Scripture calls "gods," to whom the word of God came, but before those who die "like men." And it would indeed be evil to have even a single bone of a dead man within oneself, or even some single uncleanness. But now behold the emphatic exaggeration of Scripture concerning the wickedness of hypocrites. For just as tombs are full of bones and of every uncleanness, so also those men are full of hypocrisy and iniquity, feigning not in some one matter nor in the sight of one person in all their life, or of two or three (although even this would be a most grievous evil), but they live in pretenses all the days of their life, and they are one thing while they are thought to be another. Some are lascivious within, but outwardly they show themselves to be chaste, pretenders of chastity and forgers of virginity; and others are pretenders of righteousness, while within they are wicked, and others exist as pretenders of other virtues, while within they are full of the contrary vices. There are also some who are pretenders of martyrdom, and some of the episcopate or the presbyterate or the diaconate or of ecclesiastical knowledge or of teaching, having only the masks and the outward show of virtues, but in truth being enemies of those very virtues which they feign.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 73

After this, He again derides them for vainglory, calling them "whited sepulchers" and unto all adding, "ye hypocrites;" which thing is the cause of all their evils, and the origin of their ruin. And He did not merely call them whited sepulchers, but said, that they were full of uncleanness and hypocrisy. And these things He spake, indicating the cause wherefore they did not believe, because they were full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

But these things not Christ only, but the prophets also constantly lay to their charge, that they spoil, that their rulers judge not according to the rule of justice, and every where you may find the sacrifices indeed refused, but these things required. So that there is nothing strange, nothing new, neither in the lawgiving, nor in the accusation, nay not even in the comparison of the sepulchre. For the prophet makes mention thereof, neither did he call them merely a sepulchre, "but their throat an open sepulchre."

Such are many men now also, decking themselves indeed outwardly, but full of iniquity within. For now too there is many a mode, and many a care for outward purifications, but of those in the soul not so much as one. But if indeed any one should tear open each man's conscience, many worms and much corruption would he find, and an ill savor beyond utterance; unreasonable and wicked lusts I mean, which are more unclean than worms.

But that "they" should be such persons is not "so" dreadful a thing (although it be dreadful), but that "you," that have been counted worthy to become temples of God, should of a sudden have become sepulchers, having as much ill savor, this is extreme wretchedness. He in whom Christ dwells, and the Holy Spirit hath worked, and such great mysteries, that this man should be a sepulchre, what wretchedness is this? What mournings and lamentations doth this call for, when the members of Christ have become a tomb of uncleanness? Consider how thou wast born, of what things thou hast been counted worthy, what manner of garment thou hast received, how thou wast built a temple without a breach! how fair! not adorned with gold, neither with pearls, but with the spirit that is more precious than these.

Consider that no sepulchre is made in a city, so then neither shalt thou be able to appear in the city above. For if here this is forbidden, much more there. Or rather even here thou art an object of scorn to all, bearing about a dead soul, and not to be scorned only, but also to be shunned. For tell me, if any one were to go round, bearing about a dead body, would not all have rushed away? would not all have fled? Think this now likewise. For thou goest about, bearing a spectacle far more grievous than this, a soul deadened by sins, a soul paralyzed.

Who now will pity such a one? For when thou dost not pity thine own soul, how shall another pity him that is so cruel, such an enemy to himself? If any one, where thou didst sleep and eat, had buried a dead body, what wouldest thou not have done? but thou art burying a dead soul, not where thou dinest, nor where thou sleepest, but in the members of Christ: and art thou not afraid lest a thousand lightnings and thunderbolts be hurled from above upon thine head?
Commentary on Matthew

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outside appear beautiful to men, but inside are full of the bones of the dead and of all filthiness. What he had shown in the cup and the dish, in that they were washed outside and filthy within, he now repeats through the example of tombs: that just as tombs are washed outwardly with lime and adorned with marbles and picked out with gold and colors, but within are full of the bones of the dead, so too the perverse teachers, who teach one thing and do another, display cleanness in the fashion of their dress and in humility of words, but inside are full of all filthiness and avarice and lust. In short, he expresses this very thing more plainly, adding:

So you too outwardly indeed appear just to men, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 25

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the just, and you say: if we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets. therefore you bear witness to yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets. And you, fill up the measure of your fathers. Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you flee from the judgment of Gehenna? therefore, behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and you will persecute them from city to city, that upon you may come all the just blood which is poured out upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the just to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things will come upon this generation.

As far as the surface of the text is concerned, he does not seem to threaten with sufficient reason against those who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the just. For as far as this alone goes, they were doing something praiseworthy, in that they built the tombs of the prophets and adorned the monuments of the just. They did not consent to the works of their fathers, by which those had dared to act against the prophets and the saints, especially in that they say: if we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets. How then were they worthy to incur the woe? But if someone speaks thus: as far indeed as that deed and the profession of their words go, they were not guilty, but they were culpable on account of this, that they bore witness to themselves that they were the sons of those who killed the prophets — this too is not true. For in a matter which does not fall under a man's choice, how can a man become guilty? For it is not within the choice of each individual man whose son he is, of a good man or of a bad man.
