From which it is certainly clear that he saw these things for us, not for himself, so that his vision might profit us whom divine patience still waits for with longsuffering. For what did it profit him to have seen the foul spirits before death and to have begged for a respite, when he did not receive the very respite he begged for? Let us therefore, dearest brethren, now carefully consider these things, lest our time pass away in vain, and then we seek to live for doing good when we are already being compelled to depart from the body.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 65

For it is just as a man about to go abroad called his servants, and handed over to them his goods.

And first indeed let us see why our Lord is likened to a man setting out on a journey — he who is our one Lord, of whom the Apostle says: "but for us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him" — provided, however, that we are ruled by him alone, and hold neither mammon as lord nor any of those lords who, signifying that they are many, the same Apostle mentions when he says: "for just as there are many gods and many lords". Let us therefore first inquire about his journeying, especially because there seems to be something contrary to his journeying in what he himself promises about himself to his disciples, saying: "where two or three have been gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them", likewise this: "behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age", and what the Baptist says about him (showing that he is everywhere) thus: "but in the midst of you stands one whom you do not know; he it is who comes after me". Therefore someone will say: if he stands even in the midst of those who do not know him, if "wherever two or three have been gathered together in" his "name" he is held to be among them, if through all the days of the disciples' life he is with them "until the consummation of the age", how is he set forth in this parable as journeying abroad? But in treating this we ought to take up also that which Paul says about himself: "but I, absent in body yet present in spirit, have already judged, as if present, that when you are gathered together and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, such a one as this be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ". For if the power of Jesus is gathered together with those who are gathered in his name, he does not journey away from his own but is always at hand to them. But if he is always present to all his own, how do his parables introduce him as journeying abroad?

See whether we can resolve in this way the question that is asked. For he who says to his disciples: "behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age", and likewise: "where two or three have been gathered together in my name, there am I also in the midst of them" and the rest, and who stands even in the midst of those who do not know him — he is the only-begotten of God, God the Word and wisdom and righteousness and truth and peace, who is not shut in by any bodily compass. According to this nature of his divinity he does not journey abroad; but he journeys abroad according to the dispensation of the body which he took up, according to which he was both troubled and made sorrowful, saying: "now is my soul troubled", and again: "my soul is sorrowful even unto death". But in saying these things we do not dissolve the man of the body that was assumed, since it is written in John: "every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God"; rather, we preserve to each substance its own property. For if every faithful man "who is joined to the Lord is one spirit", how much more is that man, whom Christ took up according to the dispensation of the flesh, not to be dissolved from him nor to be called other than he? And see how he says just as a man about to go abroad; for he was not a man but just as a man, and as though a man he will journey abroad — he who was everywhere according to the nature of his divinity. At the same time consider that the completion of the sentence does not seem to be written thus: just as a man journeying, so also Jesus, or thus: so also I, or thus: so also the son of man; because it is he himself who is set forth in the parable as journeying abroad as though a man. For he is not a man who is "wherever two or three have been gathered together in" his "name", nor is a man with us "all the days until the consummation of the age", nor is it a man that is present to the faithful gathered everywhere, but the divine power that was in Jesus.

We can also say the following about this passage: it is in no way contrary that this same Jesus, according to one understanding, should be everywhere, but according to another should journey abroad. For if we, "while we are in the body, journey abroad away from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight)", then in all who are in the body and journey abroad away from the Lord, the Lord also journeys abroad from them as they walk "by faith", "not by sight". But if we journey abroad "from the body" toward the Lord, then he too will be with us, and in return for the fact that we have walked "by faith", it will come about that afterward we may also walk "by sight". And by "sight" we mean the sight of the Word and of wisdom and of truth and of righteousness and of peace and of everything whatsoever that is the only-begotten of God. And you will understand the sight of the Word and the sight of wisdom when you have understood what the Apostle says: "my children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you". For understanding Christ formed in someone, you will consequently, according to a formation of this kind, see also the sight of Christ. This one, then, who as though a man set out abroad, called his servants, and handed over to them his tested money in chaste utterances — since his "utterances" are "chaste utterances, silver tried by fire, proven, purged seven times".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

This parable was spoken with respect to mercy in alms; but the one that comes after this, to them that neither in money, nor in word, nor in protection, nor in any other things whatever, are willing to assist their neighbors, but withhold all.

And wherefore can it be that this parable brings forward a king, but that a bridegroom? That thou mightest learn how close Christ is joined unto the virgins that strip themselves of their possessions; for this indeed is virginity. Wherefore Paul also makes this as a definition of the thing. "The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord;" such are his words: and, "For that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction. These things we advise," he saith.

And if in Luke the parable of the talents is otherwise put, this is to be said, that the one is really different from the other. For in that, from the one capital different degrees of increase were made, for from one pound one brought five, another ten; wherefore neither did they obtain the same recompense; but here, it is the contrary, and the crown is accordingly equal. For he that received two gave two, and he that had received the five again in like manner; but there since from the same beginning one made the greater, one the less, increase; as might be expected, in the rewards also, they do not enjoy the same.

But see Him everywhere, not requiring it again immediately. For in the case of the vineyard, He let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country; and here He committed to them the talents, and took His journey, that thou mightest learn His long-suffering. And to me He seems to say these things, to intimate the resurrection. But here it is no more a vineyard and husbandmen, but all servants. For not to rulers only, nor to Jews, but to all, doth He address His discourse. And they who bring a return unto Him confess frankly, both what is their own, and what their Master's. And the one saith, Lord, "Thou gavest me five talents;" and the other saith, "two," indicating that from Him they received the source of their gain, and they are very thankful, and reckon all to Him.

What then saith the Master? "Well done, thou good" (for this is goodness to look to one's neighbor) "and faithful servant; thou wast faithful over few things, I will set thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy Lord," meaning by this expression all blessedness.

But not so that other one, but how? "I knew that thou art a hard man, reaping where thou sowedst not, and gathering where thou strawedst not: and I was afraid, and hid thy talent: lo, there thou hast that is thine." What then the Master? "Thou oughtest to have put my money to the exchangers," that is, "thou oughtest to have spoken, to have admonished, to have advised." But are they disobedient? Yet this is nought to thee.

What could be more gentle than this? For men indeed do not so, but him that hath put out the money at usury, even him do they make also responsible to require it again. But He not so; but, Thou oughtest, He saith, to have put it out, and to have committed the requiring of it again to me. And I should have required it with increase; by increase upon the hearing, meaning the showing forth of the works. Thou oughtest to have done that which is easier, and to have left to me what is more difficult. Forasmuch then as he did not this, "Take," saith He, "the talent from him, and give it to him that hath ten talents. For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." What then is this? He that hath a gift of word and teaching to profit thereby, and useth it not, will lose the gift also; but he that giveth diligence, will gain to himself the gift in more abundance; even as the other loseth what he had received. But not to this is the penalty limited for him that is slothful, but even intolerable is the punishment, and with the punishment the sentence, which is full of a heavy accusation. For "cast ye," saith He, "the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Seest thou how not only the spoiler, and the covetous, nor only the doer of evil things, but also he that doeth not good things, is punished with extreme punishment.

Let us hearken then to these words. As we have opportunity, let us help on our salvation, let us get oil for our lamps, let us labor to add to our talent. For if we be backward, and spend our time in sloth here, no one will pity us any more hereafter, though we should wail ten thousand times. He also that had on the filthy garments condemned himself, and profited nothing. He also that had the one talent restored that which was committed to his charge, and yet was condemned. The virgins again entreated, and came unto Him and knocked, and all in vain, and without effect.

Knowing then these things, let us contribute alike wealth, and diligence, and protection, and all things for our neighbor's advantage. For the talents here are each person's ability, whether in the way of protection, or in money, or in teaching, or in what thing soever of the kind. Let no man say, I have but one talent, and can do nothing; for thou canst even by one approve thyself. For thou art not poorer than that widow; thou art not more uninstructed than Peter and John, who were both "unlearned and ignorant men;" but nevertheless, since they showed forth a zeal, and did all things for the common good, they attained to Heaven. For nothing is so pleasing to God, as to live for the common advantage.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

And wherefore can it be that this parable brings forward a king, but that a bridegroom? That thou mightest learn how close Christ is joined unto the virgins that strip themselves of their possessions; for this indeed is virginity. Wherefore Paul also makes this as a definition of the thing. "The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord;" such are his words: and, "For that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction. These things we advise," he saith.

And if in Luke the parable of the talents is otherwise put, this is to be said, that the one is really different from the other. For in that, from the one capital different degrees of increase were made, for from one pound one brought five, another ten; wherefore neither did they obtain the same recompense; but here, it is the contrary, and the crown is accordingly equal. For he that received two gave two, and he that had received the five again in like manner; but there since from the same beginning one made the greater, one the less, increase; as might be expected, in the rewards also, they do not enjoy the same.
Commentary on Matthew

For just as a man setting out on a journey called his servants and handed over his goods to them, and to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one. This man, the householder, is beyond doubt Christ, who, ascending as victor to the Father after the resurrection, called the apostles and handed over to them the teaching of the Gospel, giving more to one and less to another, not out of lavishness or stinginess but according to the strength of those who received it, just as the Apostle too says that he gave milk to drink to those who could not take solid food. In short, he receives with like joy both the one who had made ten out of five talents and the one who had made four out of two, considering not the size of the profit but the will behind the effort. In the five and the two and the one talent let us understand either the diverse graces that have been handed over to each, or else in the first all the senses tested, in the second understanding and works, in the third reason, by which we men are set apart from the beasts.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

Who then is this man who goes on a journey, if not our Redeemer, who departed into heaven in the flesh which he had assumed? For the proper place of flesh is earth, which is led as if to foreign lands when it is placed in heaven through our Redeemer. But this man going abroad handed over his goods to his servants, because he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful ones.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 66

And to one he gave five talents, but to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own capacity, and he departed. Immediately he who had received the five talents went away and worked with them and gained another five talents. Likewise also he who had received the two gained another two with them. But he who had received the one went away, dug in the earth, and hid his lord's money.

Therefore, if ever you see that, among those who have received from Christ the dispensation of the oracles of God, some indeed possess more and something more divine and more abundant, while others possess less and (so to speak) do not understand even half of the matters at hand in comparison with those who are much better, while still others possess even less — you will observe the differences among those who have received the oracles of God from Christ, since the capacity of those to whom five talents were given was one thing, and that of those to whom two were given was another, and that of those to whom one was given was another, and one did not have the measure of the other. And he who received the one talent received indeed a gift not to be despised; for even one talent of such a lord is a great thing. Yet there are three proper servants of him who went abroad as a man, just as there are also three kinds of those who bear fruit, of whom "some" indeed make "a hundred, some sixty, but some thirty". But there even he who made thirty is saved. Here, however, this discourse condemns him who had received the one talent and hid it in the earth. And I ask whether those who received five talents can be understood as the more perfect who received the more divine and loftier sense of Scripture; and those who received two rose indeed a little above the letter but were not able to ascend to that greatness; and the third ones, who received nothing above the letter which they received at first. Therefore there is, altogether, concerning the numbers in these things which we are discussing, a discourse worthy of such a Lord our Savior — I mean concerning the five and the two and the one.

But we, being of small stature and less able to unfold such things, judge that perhaps those who are able to lead all the perceptible senses of the Scriptures up to the more divine senses (which Solomon calls divine, and which Jeremiah calls the "senses of the heart", and which by Paul in the letter to the Hebrews are called "senses exercised for the discernment of good and also of evil") — these are they who, besides the five talents, gained another five, working with them and by teaching training themselves and raising themselves up to greater knowledge; for having conducted themselves in a saving manner and teaching diligently, they worked and gained another five; for no one easily receives an addition of any virtue other than of that which he has — for example, the wise man grows in wisdom, the faithful man in faith. Or thus: he acquired another five; since each one teaches to another that which he himself knows, and teaches another as much as he himself knows, no more. Therefore whatever anyone has in himself, this he acquires in another by teaching him, making him have what he himself also has. Therefore he who had the five is not said to have acquired more than the five which he had, and he who had the two, no more than the two which he had. But if we ought to speak also of the two talents, we shall speak of those as well: that they who did not remain in the letter, but seeking to ascend by their own understanding above it, yet not being able to arrive above the rank of the aforesaid two, these are they who, from him who knew their capacity, received two talents, having been taught bodily doctrine (for two seems to be the carnal number), and upon these they gained two, that is, a more bodily instruction and another a little loftier than it.

But there was a certain one of the servants gathering to himself a lesser capacity, on account of which the householder gave one talent as to one less able; and the servant, receiving it, having a certain earth, dug, and placed it in its depth, when he ought rather to have sent it up and put it upon the tables. But since three proper servants are reported to belong to that householder, I ask whether they can, after they believed and became his servants, as being capable of trading, afterward have received from the householder his money, so that one indeed both worked and gained, and another gained, but another, through fear not sufficiently faithful, buried and hid his lord's money. And it appears in his very defense, through the things which he says, that he indeed feared the lord (having the fear of God, just as another had "the zeal of God", "but not according to knowledge"), and out of fear hid his talent in the earth. Such are they who neither move nor examine the things that are said, nor give themselves over to the profiting of souls, but wish to keep hidden the things they have received and been entrusted with. If therefore you ever see anyone who has indeed acquired some capacity and has the capacity of speaking and of profiting souls to whatever degree, and hides this capacity (so that he only hands on the bare word which he was entrusted with and received as a deposit committed to him by his lord) and lives in obscurity, unknown to many even to those who have great sins, and does not bring himself forward in the good which he received from God — although he may have a certain religious manner of life not blameworthy to many — do not hesitate to say that such a one is he who received one talent and hid it in the earth.

But if, on account of that which is written, that such a one is sent "into the outer darkness", what is said displeases you — if on account of the fact that someone did not teach he is judged as one who did not use the capacity given to him for the profiting of souls — recall the apostolic saying which says: "for woe is me if I shall not have preached the Gospel".

For not on account of any other blameworthy conduct of his, but on account of this alone, if he shall not have preached the Gospel, does he confess that woe will be to him. For it manifestly appears that that man expected to hear: "wicked and slothful servant", and the rest, unless he had preached the Gospel, although the other things of his life had been upright. For these things and things like these ought especially to be held in mind by those who put "their hand", that is, their action, "to the plow" of teaching the doctrine of Christ, so that, knowing to whom woe is laid up (not on account of anything else except that they do not teach), they may not turn "back" after they have once put "their hand to the plow" that plows the souls of men, so that after this they may also receive the seeds of the word.

But this one who as a man about to go abroad called his servants and handed over to them his goods, "came after much time", after he had sent forth those fit for trading in the salvation of souls. And therefore perhaps it is not easily found that any one of those who were fit for such a work should quickly pass from this life; as is manifest from the fact that even the apostles grew old, of whom he says to Peter: "when you shall have grown old, you shall stretch out your hand", and the rest; and concerning Paul it is said to Philemon, "but now as Paul the aged", though he was a young man when Stephen was being stoned for the testimony of Christ and he himself was guarding the garments of those who were killing him. And this we have said on account of that which he says: after much time the lord of those servants came.

And observe in this place that the servants do not go to the lord, that they may be judged and receive things worthy of their deeds, but the lord comes to them,

when that which was said shall have been fulfilled: "since the time has come". And coming, he will set the account with them concerning all things whatsoever they have done, weighing the gains of good works and the losses of sins, so that, setting the account and diligently examining all things, he may deal with each one as is fitting. We ought therefore — as those who by sinning have incurred loss but by working good things gain — thus with all watchfulness to keep our hearts, so that when our lord shall have come and set the account with us, we may not be found to have incurred loss even for an idle word.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

But see Him everywhere, not requiring it again immediately. For in the case of the vineyard, He let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country; and here He committed to them the talents, and took His journey, that thou mightest learn His long-suffering. And to me He seems to say these things, to intimate the resurrection. But here it is no more a vineyard and husbandmen, but all servants. For not to rulers only, nor to Jews, but to all, doth He address His discourse.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

And to one indeed he entrusted five talents, to another two, and to another one. For there are five senses of the body, namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. By five talents, therefore, is expressed the gift of the five senses, that is, knowledge of external things. By two is designated understanding and action. By the term of one talent is designated understanding alone.
Commentary on Matthew

Then he who had received five talents went away and traded with them; he gained five more. Having received earthly senses, he doubled for himself the knowledge of heavenly things, understanding the Creator from creatures, the incorporeal from the corporeal, the invisible from the visible, the eternal from the brief.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

But he who had received five talents gained another five, because there are some who, although they do not know how to penetrate internal and mystical things, nevertheless for the sake of their intention toward the heavenly homeland teach right things to those they can from those very external things they have received; and while they guard themselves from the wantonness of the flesh and from the pursuit of earthly things and from the pleasure of visible things, they also restrain others from these by admonishing them. Moreover, it is rightly reported that another five or another two came as profit, because when preaching is expended on both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled.
Commentary on Matthew

He who had received two; he gained two more. This one too, according to his strength, doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the law; or else he understood both the knowledge and the works of the present life as types of the future blessedness.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

And there are some who, as if enriched with two talents, receive understanding and action, understand subtle things about internal matters, work wonders in external things; and when by both understanding and working they preach to others, they bring back, as it were, a doubled profit from their business. Moreover, it is rightly reported that another five or another two came as profit, because when preaching is expended on both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled.
Commentary on Matthew

But he who had received one went off, dug in the earth and hid his lord's money. The wicked servant, by earthly works and the pleasure of the world, neglected and defiled the commandments of God; although in another evangelist it is written that he tied it up in a napkin, that is, that by living softly and delicately he enfeebled the teaching of the householder.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

But he who had received one talent went away, dug in the earth, and hid his lord's money. To hide the talent in the earth is to involve the received ability in earthly activities, not to seek spiritual profit, never to lift the heart from earthly thoughts. For there are some who have received the gift of understanding, but nevertheless think only of the things of the flesh. Of whom it is said through the prophet: They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good.
Commentary on Matthew

But after a long time the lord of those servants came. A great time lies between the ascension of the Savior and his second coming. But if the apostles are to render an account and to rise again under fear of the judge, what ought we to do?
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

But the Lord who conferred the talents returns to settle accounts, because he who now piously grants spiritual gifts strictly examines merits in judgment, considers what each one received, and weighs what profit one brings back from what was received.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 67

And the one who had received the five talents came forward and presented another five talents, saying: Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five besides. His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord. And the one also who had received the two talents came forward and said: Lord, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained another two. His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord.

Thus the first came forward as one who had confidence in that he had labored and gained; for that very confidence made him bold, so that he was the first to come to the lord and to make his speech boldly, saying: Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five talents upon them. To him the lord spoke a word desirable to all of us, when our Lord shall have settled the account also with us, saying: Well done, good and faithful servant, the opposite of that word which he said to the third: wicked and slothful servant. Who would not wish, receiving exhortation from this scripture, that he might hear from his lord: faithful, which I judge to be like that which was said of Abraham, that "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him unto righteousness". So also for him who heard from his lord: faithful servant, without doubt his faith was reckoned to him unto righteousness, just as the faith of that very man was reckoned unto righteousness, who was faithful in a little (and all the things of this life are little), so that the whole mystery of the resurrection might be entrusted to him, and the administration of the goods on high.

But let us also see whither this good and faithful servant enters, who was faithful in the little of this life. Enter, he says, into the joy of your lord. For all things there are delightful and all things joys, when those who weep here shall laugh there, and those who mourn in praiseworthy fashion shall receive worthy consolation. But as to what he says (whether in the case of the one who had received five talents, or of this one who had received two): coming forward, understand for me the approach and passage from this world to that one, and see that the lord uttered to the second no other word than the one he uttered to the former, saying: Well done, good and faithful servant, you have been faithful over the little, I will set you over the great. And I ask, since the same things were said to both. Perhaps even the one who had the lesser virtue and exercised the whole of it, as much as he had, according to what was fitting, is to have nothing less with God than the one who was in greater virtue, so that in them may be fulfilled what was said: "He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack". Something of this kind is shown also concerning the commandment of love toward God and toward the neighbor, when it says thus: "You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with your whole strength". For without doubt, when anyone shall have loved God "with his whole heart" "and with his whole soul" "and with his whole strength", he has such a reward of love as the one who had a greater heart, or who has a more eminent soul, or who received greater strength. For this alone is sought, that whatever a man may have from God, he should use the whole of it for the glory of God.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

And they who bring a return unto Him confess frankly, both what is their own, and what their Master's. And the one saith, Lord, "Thou gavest me five talents;" and the other saith, "two," indicating that from Him they received the source of their gain, and they are very thankful, and reckon all to Him.

What then saith the Master? "Well done, thou good" (for this is goodness to look to one's neighbor) "and faithful servant; thou wast faithful over few things, I will set thee over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy Lord," meaning by this expression all blessedness.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 6: 'WELL DONE, WELL DONE' AS PRAISE AND AS MOCKERY

What does it mean when David says, "Let them be confused and ashamed who say to me, 'Well done, well done'" (Ps. 69:4), while the Lord says, "Well done, good and faithful servant" (Matt. 25:21, 23), etc.? That which David took as something bad, the Savior shows to be worthy of good merits. — This does not differ much from the previous question. For one and the same word has different meanings, as I mentioned above. For the detractors of David, since they supported his destruction, were rejoicing at his misfortunes. While he was suffering pressures and distresses from Saul and from his son Absalom, they said that this was rightly and well done to him. It is like when someone says, of a man who is suffering wrongs, "It serves him right"; that is, to rejoice in another's troubles: this is to say, "He is getting what he deserves." In a similar way, the Savior, rejoicing in good works, proclaims a man's merit by saying, "Well done, good and faithful servant." For he exults because the servant has made himself more worthy, saying, "Well done," that is, "You have acted rightly, so that you might place yourself in a position of greater merit." Therefore one word is applied to two opposite causes. For we are accustomed to say of someone, "He has been judged." But how it is said is made clear by the cause that either follows or precedes. For sometimes it is said with reference to good, sometimes to evil; just as desire is sometimes directed to good, sometimes to evil.
Commentary on Matthew

His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your lord. To both servants, as I have already said before, both the one who had made ten out of five talents and the one who had made four out of two, the same word of the householder speaks kindly. And it is to be noted that all the things we have in the present, though they seem great and very many, are yet small and few in comparison with the things to come. Enter, he says, into the joy of your lord, and receive what neither eye has seen nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. But what greater thing can be given to a faithful servant than to be with his lord and to see the joy of his lord?
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

The servant who returned the doubled talents is praised by the master and led to eternal reward, when it is said to him by the Lord's voice: "Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord." For all the goods of the present life are few things, however many they may seem, in comparison with the eternal reward. But then the faithful servant is set over many things when, having overcome all the trouble of corruption, he is glorified in that heavenly seat with eternal joys. Then he is perfectly admitted into the joy of his lord, when, taken up into that eternal homeland and mingled with the company of angels, he so rejoices inwardly at the gift that there is no longer anything to grieve him outwardly from corruption.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 68

But he also who had received the one talent came and said: Lord, I know that you are a hard man, and you reap where you have not sown, and you gather where you have not scattered; and being afraid I went away, and hid your talent in the earth: behold, you have what is yours. But his lord answering said to him: You wicked and slothful servant, you knew that I reap where I have not sown, and gather where I have not scattered? You ought therefore to have committed my money to the money-changers, so that at my coming I might have received it back with interest.

It seems to me that this man who received the one talent was indeed among the believers, yet not among those acting with confidence in the faith, but rather wishing to hide themselves and doing everything so as not to be recognized as Christians. But perhaps in other respects too their conduct was not sufficiently blameworthy, and what they received they do indeed keep but do not also add to it, neither do they trade with it nor act confidently in it; and therefore the word in them did not advance to something greater nor gain others. Furthermore, those who are of this sort seem to me to have a fear of God and to think of Him as of one austere and hard and implacable; for the very words of the one answering and saying signify this: I knew that you are hard, and as one who knew that He reaps where He did not sow and gathers where He did not scatter. On which account his lord answering him and rebuking him as a wicked and slothful servant, did not indeed confess Himself to be a hard man, as that man supposed, but consented to his other words, saying to him: You knew that I reap where I have not sown, and gather where I have not scattered?

But how are we to understand that our Lord truly reaps where He did not sow, and gathers where He did not scatter? To me it seems thus in this place: that since the righteous man "sows in the spirit", from which also "he shall reap eternal life". But all things which are sown by another (that is, by a righteous man) and reaped unto eternal life, God reaps; for the righteous man is God's possession, who reaps where He Himself did not sow but that righteous man sowed. Consequently we shall also say this, that since the righteous man "has dispersed, has given to the poor", the Lord will gather into Himself all things whatsoever the righteous man "has dispersed and given to the poor". And reaping the things He did not sow and gathering where He did not scatter, He reckons to Himself and considers to have been conferred upon Himself whatsoever shall have been sown or scattered upon the faithful poor, saying to those who have done well to their neighbors: "Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom which is prepared for you. For I was hungry and you gave me to eat" and the rest.

And because He wishes to reap where He did not sow and to gather where He did not scatter, when He shall not have found it, He will say to those who did not furnish Him something to reap and to gather: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me to eat" and the rest. For indeed He is truly hard (according to what Matthew says) and "austere" (according to what Luke said), but to those who abuse the mercy of God unto their own negligence and not unto their own conversion, as the Apostle says: "Behold the goodness of God and the severity; toward those indeed who fell, severity, but toward you, goodness, if you shall remain in goodness". For whoever judges God to be good, believing that he will receive pardon if he shall have been converted to Him, to that man God is good. But whoever esteems Him so good that He cares nothing about the sins of sinners, to that man God is not good but hard and "austere"; for He is zealous over the sins of men who despise Him. Yet, since Christ reaps, as it were, what we have sown and gathers what we have scattered,

let us sow "in the spirit" and scatter "to the poor" and let us not hide God's talent in the earth.

For a fear of this kind is not good, nor does such fear free us from those outer darknesses, when we shall have been condemned as wicked and slothful servants:

wicked indeed, because we have not used that tested money of the Lord's words, with which we could have traded and examined the utterances of Christianity and acquired the deeper mysteries of the goodness of God; but slothful, because we have not worked with the utterances of God for salvation, whether our own or others'.

Since we ought to send the money of our Lord, that is, the utterances, to hearers who are money-changers, who try and test all things, so that they may hold fast the good and true teaching, but reject the reprobate and false,

so that when the Lord shall come, He may receive back those utterances, which we have committed, with interest and with additions from those who received them from us.

For every coin, that is, every word which has in itself the royal form of God and the image of His word, is genuine.

He commands, therefore, that the word be entrusted to men who are money-changers, who are able to render its interest. And he renders the interest of the word who hastens to save another together with himself, just as he himself was saved: as Andrew saved Peter, Philip Nathanael, Matthew the publicans. And this is what the Apostle says: "The things you have heard from me through many witnesses, these commend to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others also". Likewise the Lord also says: "No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

But not so that other one, but how? "I knew that thou art a hard man, reaping where thou sowedst not, and gathering where thou strawedst not: and I was afraid, and hid thy talent: lo, there thou hast that is thine." What then the Master? "Thou oughtest to have put my money to the exchangers," that is, "thou oughtest to have spoken, to have admonished, to have advised." But are they disobedient? Yet this is nought to thee.

What could be more gentle than this? For men indeed do not so, but him that hath put out the money at usury, even him do they make also responsible to require it again. But He not so; but, Thou oughtest, He saith, to have put it out, and to have committed the requiring of it again to me. And I should have required it with increase; by increase upon the hearing, meaning the showing forth of the works. Thou oughtest to have done that which is easier, and to have left to me what is more difficult.
Commentary on Matthew

And he too who had received one talent came forward and said: Lord, I know that you are a hard man; you reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter; and being afraid I went off and hid your talent in the earth; here you have what is yours. Truly, what is written: To make excuses in sins, befell this servant also, so that to sloth and negligence the charge of pride was added as well. For he who ought simply to have confessed his idleness and entreated the householder, on the contrary slanders him and says that he acted on prudent counsel, lest while he sought profit on the money he should put even the principal at risk.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

The servant, however, who refused to work with his talent, returns to his master with words of excuse, saying: "Lord, I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you did not scatter; and being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the ground; behold, you have what is yours." It should be noted that the useless servant calls his master hard, yet pretends not to serve him for gain, and says he was afraid to spend the talent for profit, when he should have feared only this: that he might return it to his master without profit. For there are many within the holy Church, whose image this servant represents, who fear to undertake the ways of a better life, and yet do not fear to lie in the sloth of their torpor; and when they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to seize upon the ways of holiness, yet do not dread remaining in their iniquities. Peter, while still placed in weakness, well represents the likeness of these when, upon seeing the miracle of the fish, he said: "Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man." On the contrary, if you consider yourself a sinner, you ought not to repel the Lord from yourself. But those who refuse to grasp the ways of a better habit and the citadel of a more upright life because they perceive themselves to be weak, as it were both confess themselves sinners and repel the Lord, and flee from Him whom they ought to have sanctified in themselves; and as if having no counsel in their confusion, they die while fearing life.
Commentary on Matthew

But his lord answered and said to him: Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter; you ought therefore to have put my money with the money-changers, and on coming I would surely have received what is mine with interest; take therefore the talent from him and give it to him who has ten talents. What he had thought he said by way of excuse is turned into his own guilt. He is called a wicked servant because he slanders his lord, lazy because he would not double the talent, so that in the one he is condemned for pride, in the other for negligence. If, he says, you knew that I am hard and cruel, and that I go after what belongs to others and reap there where I have not sown, why did not a thought of this kind strike fear into you, so that you would know that I would seek out my own more diligently, and would give my money, or silver, to the money-changers? For the Greek word ἀργύριον signifies both. The words, he says, of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved, purged of earth sevenfold. The money, then, and the silver is the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been given to the money-changers and bankers, that is, either to the other teachers, as the apostles also did, ordaining presbyters and bishops in the several provinces, or to all believers who can double the money and return it with interest, so that whatever they had learned by word they might fulfill in deed. Now the talent is taken away and given to him who had made ten talents, so that we may understand that, although the Lord's joy over the labor of both is equal, that is, both of him who had doubled five into ten and of him who had doubled two into four, yet a greater reward is owed to him who had labored more over the Lord's money. Hence the Apostle too says: Honor the presbyters who are truly presbyters, especially those who labor in the word of God. From the fact that the wicked servant dared to say: you reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter, we understand that the Lord accepts the good life even of Gentiles and philosophers, and regards in one way those who act justly and in another those who act unjustly, and that, in comparison with him who serves the natural law, those who neglect the written law are condemned.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

Hence this servant is immediately answered: "Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow, and gather where I did not scatter; therefore you ought to have given my money to the bankers, and upon my coming I would have received what is mine with interest." The servant is bound by his own words when the master says: "I reap where I did not sow, and gather where I did not scatter." As if he were openly saying: If according to your judgment I even demand what I did not give, how much more do I demand from you what I gave to be distributed; therefore you ought to have given my money to the bankers, and upon my coming I would have received what is mine with interest. To give money to the bankers is to impart the knowledge of preaching to those who are able to exercise it.

But just as you see our peril if we withhold the Lord's money, so carefully consider your own peril, dearest brothers, because what you hear is demanded back from you with interest. For in usury, money is received back even though it was not given. For when that which was received is returned, something additional is paid beyond what was received. Consider therefore, dearest brothers, that you will pay interest on this money of the word you have received, and take care that from what you hear you also strive to understand other things which you do not hear, so that by gathering some things from others, you may also learn to do from yourselves those things which you have not yet learned from the mouth of the preacher.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 69

Take away from him therefore the talent, and give it to the one who has ten talents. You see that the talent is taken away from the wicked and lazy servant, and given to the one who has ten talents. But how something is taken away from someone which had been given to him, and given to another who acts well, so that he may have these things also on top of those which he had acquired — this is not very easy to explain. Yet it is possible, since he who makes a faculty in someone apt in the doctrines of truth can, by his own divinity, God taking away the sufficiency from the one who has used it too lazily, give it to the one who has multiplied it.

For to everyone who has it shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him who has not, even that which he has shall be taken away from him. For example, to one who has faith, even that which is from ourselves, shall be given the grace of faith which is from God through the spirit of faith, and he shall have abundance; and whatever anyone has from his natural creation, when he has exercised it, he receives that very thing also from the grace of God, so that he may have abundance and be more firm in that very thing which he has.

For it is to be understood by us not concerning wisdom alone, but concerning every virtue, what Solomon says: "and even if anyone be perfect among the sons of men, if your wisdom be absent from him, he shall be reckoned as nothing". So too whoever has been perfect in chastity or in righteousness or in virtue or in piety, but there has not been in him either the chastity or the righteousness or the virtue or the piety which comes from the grace of God, such a man is reckoned "as nothing". Therefore, if we wish that a more perfect virtue be given to us and abound in us, let us by all means acquire through diligence that which is perfect among men; and after we have acquired it, understanding as it were that these things are reckoned as nothing without the grace of God, let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and let us pray lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute, so that the perfection of all the good things that are in us may be given from God, and that he may make us perfect and acceptable to God as sons of God.

But this man who had received one talent and had hidden it in the earth, is not only reproved as wicked and lazy, but is sent as useless into the outer darkness, where perhaps there is no illumination, neither bodily, nor is there any regard of God there;

but as unworthy of the contemplation of God, those who have committed such sins are condemned in these places which are called the outer darkness: perhaps until they understand, so that they may be converted and be made worthy to go out from them; perhaps also for another cause (which we do not know), since we read that someone who was before us expounding about the darkness of the abyss and saying that the abyss is outside the world, without, and darkness. Let us therefore consider whether his exposition can be true, that we should understand those outer darknesses in such a way that certain ones, as unworthy of the whole world, are cast out into that abyss (which he expounded), without, in which there is darkness, with no one illuminating it, since they are outside the whole world.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

Forasmuch then as he did not this, "Take," saith He, "the talent from him, and give it to him that hath ten talents. For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." What then is this? He that hath a gift of word and teaching to profit thereby, and useth it not, will lose the gift also; but he that giveth diligence, will gain to himself the gift in more abundance; even as the other loseth what he had received.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

But let us hear with what sentence he strikes the lazy servant: Take the talent from him, and give it to him who has ten talents.

It seemed very fitting that when the one talent is taken from the wicked servant, it should be given rather to the one who had received two talents than to the one who had received five. For it ought to have been given to the one who had less rather than to the one who had more. But, as we said above, by the five talents is signified knowledge of external things, that is, the five senses; while by the two talents are expressed understanding and action. Therefore the one who had received two talents had more than the one who had received five, because he who through the five talents merited the administration of external things was still empty of understanding of internal things. Therefore the one talent, which we said signifies understanding, ought to have been given to the one who had well administered the external things he had received. This we see daily in the holy Church, because many, while they well administer the external things they receive, are led through added grace also to mystical understanding, so that those who faithfully administer external things also excel in internal understanding.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER TWO

[Daniel 2:21] "And it is He who changes times and seasons, who transfers kingdoms and establishes kingdoms." Let us not marvel, therefore, whenever we see kings and empires succeed one another, for it is by the will of God that they are governed, altered, and terminated. And the cases of individuals are well known to Him who founded all things. He often permits wicked kings to arise in order that they may in their wickedness punish the wicked. At the same time by indirect suggestion and general discussion he prepares the reader for the fact that the dream Nebuchadnezzar saw was concerned with the change and succession of empires. "He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who acquire learning." This accords with the scripture: "The wise man will hear and increase his wisdom" (Proverbs 1:5). "For he who has, to him it shall be given" (Matthew 25:29). A soul which cherishes an ardent love of wisdom is freely infilled by the Spirit of God. But wisdom will never penetrate a perverse soul (Wisdom 3:1-13).
Commentary on Matthew

For to everyone who has will be given, and he will abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away from him. Many, though they are wise by nature and have keenness of mind, if they have been negligent and have spoiled the good of nature by sloth, in comparison with one who is somewhat slower but has made up by labor and diligence for what he had less of, lose the good of nature and see the reward that had been promised them pass to others. It can also be understood thus: to him who has faith and a good will in the Lord, even if, being a man, he has had something less in works, it will be given by the good judge; but he who has not had faith will lose even the other virtues that he seemed to possess by nature. And elegantly too: even what he seems, he says, to have will be taken away from him. For whatever is without faith in Christ ought not to be credited to him who has badly misused it, but to him who granted the good of nature even to a wicked servant.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

A general statement is also immediately added, in which it is said: "For to everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him." For to him who has it shall be given, and he shall abound, because whoever has charity also receives other gifts. Whoever does not have charity loses even the gifts he seemed to have received. Therefore it is necessary, my brothers, that in everything you do, you watch over the keeping of charity. True charity is to love a friend in God, and to love an enemy for the sake of God. Whoever does not have this loses every good thing he has, is deprived of the talent he had received, and according to the Lord's sentence is cast into the outer darkness.
On the Resurrection of the Flesh

He affirms, lastly, that "the very hairs of our head are all numbered," and in the affirmation He of course includes the promise of their safety; for if they were to be lost, where would be the use of having taken such a numerical care of them? Surely the only use lies (in this truth): "That of all which the Father hath given to me, I should lose none," -not even a hair, as also not an eye nor a tooth. And yet whence shall come that "weeping and gnashing of teeth," if not from eyes and teeth?-even at that time when the body shall be slain in hell, and thrust out into that outer darkness which shall be the suitable torment of the eyes.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 78

But not to this is the penalty limited for him that is slothful, but even intolerable is the punishment, and with the punishment the sentence, which is full of a heavy accusation. For "cast ye," saith He, "the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Seest thou how not only the spoiler, and the covetous, nor only the doer of evil things, but also he that doeth not good things, is punished with extreme punishment.

Let us hearken then to these words. As we have opportunity, let us help on our salvation, let us get oil for our lamps, let us labor to add to our talent. For if we be backward, and spend our time in sloth here, no one will pity us any more hereafter, though we should wail ten thousand times. He also that had on the filthy garments condemned himself, and profited nothing. He also that had the one talent restored that which was committed to his charge, and yet was condemned. The virgins again entreated, and came unto Him and knocked, and all in vain, and without effect.

Knowing then these things, let us contribute alike wealth, and diligence, and protection, and all things for our neighbor's advantage. For the talents here are each person's ability, whether in the way of protection, or in money, or in teaching, or in what thing soever of the kind. Let no man say, I have but one talent, and can do nothing; for thou canst even by one approve thyself. For thou art not poorer than that widow; thou art not more uninstructed than Peter and John, who were both "unlearned and ignorant men;" but nevertheless, since they showed forth a zeal, and did all things for the common good, they attained to Heaven. For nothing is so pleasing to God, as to live for the common advantage.
Commentary on Matthew

And cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The Lord is light. Whoever is sent out by him lacks the true light. But what the weeping and gnashing of teeth is, we have said above.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 9

For through punishment he falls into the outer darkness who through his own fault willingly fell into inner darkness; and there he suffers unwillingly the darkness of vengeance, who here willingly endured the darkness of pleasure.

It must be known that no lazy person is secure from this receiving of the talent. For there is no one who can truly say: "I have received no talent at all, there is nothing for which I can be compelled to give account." For by the name of talent, even this very thing will be reckoned to any poor person—that he received even the least thing. For one person received understanding; he owes the ministry of preaching from his talent. Another received earthly substance; he owes the distribution of his talent from his possessions. Another received neither understanding of interior things nor abundance of possessions, but nevertheless learned an art by which he is fed; that very art is reckoned to him as the receiving of a talent. Another has attained none of these things, but nevertheless has perhaps earned a place of familiarity with a rich person; he has certainly received the talent of familiarity. If therefore he says nothing to him on behalf of the needy, he is condemned for retaining his talent. Therefore let him who has understanding take care by all means not to be silent; let him who has abundance of possessions watch lest he grow sluggish in the generosity of mercy; let him who has an art by which he is governed strive greatly to share its use and benefit with his neighbor; let him who has a place of speaking with a rich person fear condemnation for the retained talent if, when he is able, he does not intercede with him on behalf of the poor. For the coming Judge will require from each one of us as much as He gave. Therefore, that each person may be secure concerning the accounts of his talent when the Lord returns, let him consider daily with trembling what he has received. For behold, He who departed on a journey is now near to returning. For He went as if on a journey when He departed far from this earth on which He was born; but He certainly returns to settle accounts for the talents, because if we grow sluggish from good action, He judges us more strictly concerning those very gifts which He bestowed. Let us therefore consider what we have received, and let us be vigilant in their distribution. Let no earthly care impede us from spiritual work, lest if the talent is hidden in the earth, the lord of the talent be provoked to anger. For the lazy servant lifts the talent from the earth when the Judge is now examining his faults, because there are many who only withdraw themselves from earthly desires or works when they are already being dragged to eternal punishment by the judgment of the Judge. Let us therefore be vigilant beforehand concerning the account to be rendered for our talent, so that when the Judge now looms to strike, the profit we have made may excuse us.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 70

But when the Son of Man shall come in his glory, and all the angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory; and before him shall be gathered all the nations, and the rest. Taken without examination, the passage seems plain, as though it were exhorting people to give and to be generous and turning them away from all inhumanity and stinginess. Let us see, nevertheless, what one ought to look for in it, for the sake of those who suppose there is nothing else in it but an exhortation to kindness. Certainly the whole Church believes that there will be a second and glorious coming of Christ, when the Son of God also, "who was taken up in glory," will thus return here with glory in his own form and his own beauty, so that his body will be such as it was when he had been transfigured on the mountain before the three disciples who had climbed up with him — so that now he may appear before not three, nor a few others, but all the nations gathered together. And he shall sit upon the throne of his glory, and then he shall separate the evil from the good — whether, however, all from all who have existed in all the generations, or only those … who shall have been left at the consummation, or only those who have believed in God through Christ, and of these too whether all or not all, is not sufficiently clear. Yet to some it seems that these things are said concerning the distinction among those who have believed. As far, then, as the plain text goes, those who stand at the right hand are praised and called into the prepared kingdom for no other reason than kindness alone, nor are those who are at the left hand put to shame and consigned to the fire for any other reason than inhumanity. What then? If these who have been kind were negligent as regards the other virtues, will they attain such promises as these? Or will those who were not kind, if they fulfilled the other virtues, be cursed altogether and be condemned to the fire, and this together with the devil himself? You see, then, that the passage requires wisdom.

Likewise it must be discussed whether the Savior's coming in glory will take place in a place, or whether we ought to seek out another interpretation. For what place will that be, such as to contain in one view both all the angels coming with Christ and all the nations gathered there? And what is to be said about the throne of his glory? Do you think there will be some bodily seat, or does this too require a more subtle interpretation? Therefore he who wishes to understand all things rationally will find much wisdom in these matters as well; and it is indeed dangerous to expound on things of this kind. But lest, by keeping fuller silence on account of the difficulty of the meaning, we abandon those who are moved by these things to be tossed about, let us expound a few things out of many (as far as it is possible). I judge, therefore, that there will be a time of Christ's coming, when so great a manifestation of Christ and of his divinity will occur, that not only none of the righteous, but not even any of sinners will be ignorant of Christ "according to what he is" — when even sinners will recognize their own sins in their own sight, and the righteous will manifestly see to what an end the seeds of their righteousness have led them. And this is what he says: before him shall be gathered all the nations. For if now, when not all recognize Christ "according to what he is," nor do those who seem to recognize him recognize him openly, but people enter into his sight only in faith, when they receive the knowledge of him through faith — as it is written: "enter into his sight in exultation" — how much more rightly are all the nations said to be about to be gathered and set before him, when he has been made manifest to all, both good and evil, both faithful and unfaithful, and before the eyes of their mind is now found not by any inquiry of faith or diligence, but is brought forth by the manifestation of his very divinity?

The Son of God, when he shall have come in his glory, will not indeed appear in one place and not appear in another; but just as he himself willed to demonstrate his coming by comparison with lightning that goes forth, saying: "if they say to you: behold, he is in the desert, do not go out; behold, he is in the house, do not believe; for as lightning goes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man." "As," therefore, lightning "going forth from the east," because it fills all things, "appears even to the west," so when Christ shall have come in his glory, because he is to be everywhere. And he himself will be everywhere in the sight of all, and all will everywhere be in his sight, and thus they will be set before the throne of his glory — that is, before his kingdom and the power of his dominion. And his throne — either certainly some of the more perfect of the saints are meant (of whom it is written: "for there thrones sat in judgment"), or certain angelic powers (of whom it is said: "whether thrones or dominions"). Therefore the king of the ages, God the Word, who was also made in the form of a man, shall sit upon such a throne of his glory; and all the nations shall be gathered to him, no longer dispersed in false and manifold doctrines about him, and thus they will be before him, so that we do not hear that all the nations come to be before him in a local sense, just as neither do we hear in a local sense that the righteous will say to him the things they are going to say. As long, then, as the wicked are confounded, recognizing neither themselves nor Christ, but are held darkened in their errors, and as long as the righteous see "through a mirror and in an enigma" and know themselves "in part" — not according to what they truly are — for so long the good are not separated from the evil. But when, on account of the manifestation of the Son of God, all have come to understanding of themselves, then the Savior shall separate the good from the evil.

Now those who are saved are called sheep because of their meekness,

which they learned from him who says: "learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart," and because "even unto slaughter" they were ready to come, imitating Christ, who "was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the one shearing it, without voice" — and not simply "without voice," but "before the one shearing it, without voice," that is, before the one taking away what is his own and plundering it.

But the evil are called goats, who evilly climb the rough and hard crags

and walk along their precipices. So understand for me also the saints at the right hand, who have done works of the right hand and have been more fully turned toward righteousness, which is always at the right hand of God. Therefore, according to the worth of their right-hand deeds, they stand at the right hand, and they have received as the reward of their right-hand deeds the right hand of the king, in which is rest and glory. But those who by the perversity of their life separated themselves from the right hand, because of their worst and left-handed works, fell to the left — that is, condemned into the sorrow of torments — and for this reason they stand at the left hand. Then the king will say to those who are at the right hand, inviting them to himself: come, so that whatever had been lacking to them they may attain when they have been more perfectly united to Christ, hearing: come, and doing it. Such also is what he says in Luke: "take the talent from him, and give it to him who has ten. For everyone who has, to him it shall be added; but he who does not have, even that which he seems to have shall be taken from him." And he calls them blessed of the Father, with the addition blessed of my Father, so that the eminence of their blessing may be made manifest, who are blessed by the Lord "who made heaven and earth" — and perhaps because there are some lesser blessed ones, who are indeed blessed but not of the Father.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

"When the Son of Man shall come in His glory." For now is He come in dishonor, now in affronts and reproaches; but then shall He sit upon the throne of His glory.

And continually doth He make mention of glory. For since the cross was near, a thing that seemed to be matter of reproach, for this cause He raises up the hearer; and brings before his sight the judgment seat, and setteth round him all the world.

And not in this way only doth He make His discourse awful, but also by showing the Heavens opened. For all the angels will be present with Him, He saith, themselves also to bear witness, in how many things they had ministered, when sent by the Lord for the salvation of men.
Commentary on Matthew

But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the seat of his majesty, and all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, and he will set the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left. About to keep the Passover after two days, and to be handed over to the cross, and to be mocked by men, and to be given vinegar and gall to drink, he rightly promises the glory of one in triumph, so that he might offset the stumbling blocks that were to follow with the reward of the promise. And it is to be noted that he who is to be seen in majesty is the Son of Man.
On Modesty

Why, do you yourself, when introducing into the church, for the purpose of melting the brotherhood by his prayers, the repentant adulterer, lead into the midst and prostrate him, all in haircloth and ashes, a compound of disgrace and horror, before the widows, before the elders, suing for the tears of all, licking the footprints of all, clasping the knees of all? And do you, good shepherd and blessed father that you are, to bring about the (desired) end of the man, grace your harangue with all the allurements of mercy in your power, and under the parable of the "ewe" go in quest of your goats? do you, for fear lest your "ewe" again take a leap out from the flock-as if that were no more lawful for the future which was not even once lawful-fill all the rest likewise full of apprehension at the very moment of granting indulgence? And would the apostle so carelessly have granted indulgence to the atrocious licentiousness of fornication burdened with incest, as not at least to have exacted from the criminal even this legally established garb of repentance which you ought to have learned from him? as to have uttered no commination on the past? no allocution touching the future? Nay, more; he goes further, and beseeches that they "would confirm toward him affection," as if he were making satisfaction to him, not as if he were granting an indulgence! And yet I hear (him speak of) "affection," not "communion; "as (he writes) withal to the Thessalonians "But if any obey not our word through the epistle, him mark; and associate not with him, that he may feel awed; not regarding (him) as an enemy, but rebuking as a brother.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

And everything will help to render that day fearful. Then, "shall be gathered together," He saith, "all nations," that is, the whole race of men. "And He shall separate them one from another, as the shepherd his sheep." For now they are not separated, but all mingled together, but the division then shall be made with all exactness. And for a while it is by their place that He divides them, and makes them manifest; afterwards by the names He indicates the dispositions of each, calling the one kids, the other sheep, that He might indicate the unfruitfulness of the one, for no fruit will come from kids; and the great profit from the other, for indeed from sheep great is the profit, as well from the milk, as from the wool, and from the young, of all which things the kid is destitute.

But while the brutes have from nature their unfruitfulness, and fruitfulness, these have it from choice, wherefore some are punished, and the others crowned.
Commentary on Matthew

And what follows: he will set the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left, understand according to what you read elsewhere: The heart of the wise man is in his right hand, and the heart of the fool in his left, and above in this same Gospel: Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing. The sheep, on the side of the just, are bidden to stand at the right; the goats, that is, sinners, at the left, goats being always offered for sin in the law. Nor did he say she-goats, which can bear young and, when shorn, come up from the washing, all with twin offspring, and there is no barren one among them, but goats, a wanton and butting animal, always burning for coupling.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 71

Receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world. (What in the Latin reads from the foundation of the world, in the Greek reads thus: from the laying-down of the world; and he expounds according to the Greek expression what according to the Latin it was not fitting to expound.) But why the Scriptures frequently use the term "laying-down" in reference to the world — as here too, saying from the laying-down of the world — let him inquire who is able, knowing that not everything which has been created is called a "laying-down," nor is it written anywhere of "the laying-down" of the thrones or dominions or principalities. But if one gathers together the term "laying-down" from all its occurrences, in case perhaps it has been said in some other place, and compares those places with the things that are said about the laying-down of the world, ascending by the Word to the rest of the things that are indeed created but not "laid down" — from the fact that their creation is not a "laying-down" — you will see the reason for this so-named "laying-down," a term which is applied only to the world. But to entrust such matters as these to writings which can also come into the hands of men of evil conduct and of slanderers and of lovers of novelty is not a religious thing to do, so that pearls too elaborately wrought may not be cast before swine, nor holy things given to dogs.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

Of what honor, of what blessedness are these words? And He said not, Take, but, "Inherit," as one's own, as your Father's, as yours, as due to you from the first. For, before you were, saith He, these things had been prepared, and made ready for you, forasmuch as I knew you would be such as you are.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

Then, in order that thou mayest see in another way also the justice of the sentence, He first praises them that have done right, and saith, "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world. For I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat," and all that follows. For that they may not say, we had it not, He condemns them by their fellow-servants; like as the virgins by the virgins, and the servant that was drunken and gluttonous by the faithful servant, and him that buried his talent, by them that brought the two, and each one of them that continue in sin, by them that have done right.

And here, however, it is of an equal; for he compares rich with rich, and poor with poor. And not in this way only doth He show the sentence justly passed, by their fellow-servants having done what was right when in the same circumstances, but also by their not being obedient so much as in these things in which poverty was no hindrance; as, for instance, in giving drink to the thirsty, in looking upon him that is in bonds, in visiting the sick. And when He had commended them that had done right, He shows how great was originally His bond of love towards them. For, "Come," saith He, "ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." To how many good things is this same equivalent, to be blessed, and blessed of the Father? And wherefore were they counted worthy of such great honors? What is the cause? "I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink;" and what follows.
Commentary on Matthew
Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. This is to be taken according to the foreknowledge of God, with whom future things are already done.
Against Heresies (Book IV, Chapter 30), Section 3

And therefore has the Lord said: "Judge not, that ye be not judged: for with what judgment ye shall judge, ye shall be judged." [Matthew 7:1-2] [The meaning is] not certainly that we should not find fault with sinners, nor that we should consent to those who act wickedly; but that we should not pronounce an unfair judgment on the dispensations of God, inasmuch as He has Himself made provision that all things shall turn out for good, in a way consistent with justice. For, because He knew that we would make a good use of our substance which we should possess by receiving it from another, He says, "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." [Luke 3:11] And, "For I was an hungered, and ye gave Me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave Me drink; I was naked and ye clothed Me." [Matthew 25:35-36] And, "When thou doest thine alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." [Matthew 6:3] And we are proved to be righteous by whatsoever else we do well, redeeming, as it were, our property from strange hands. But thus do I say, "from strange hands," not as if the world were not God's possession, but that we have gifts of this sort, and receive them from others, in the same way as these men had them from the Egyptians who knew not God; and by means of these same do we erect in ourselves the tabernacle of God: for God dwells in those who act uprightly, as the Lord says: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, that they, when ye shall be put to flight," may receive you into eternal tabernacles. For whatsoever we acquired from unrighteousness when we were heathen, we are proved righteous, when we have become believers, by applying it to the Lord's advantage.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 72

I was hungry and you gave me to eat, and so on.

It seems to me through these words that not one single kind of righteousness is rewarded, as many suppose. For it is absurd to understand nothing else of virtue in the one who is thus rewarded except only the sharing of human kindness.
